explanation: The output frequency of an AC generator is determined by the speed of the rotor and the number of pole pairs. Therefore, the frequency is directly dependent on the speed of the rotor and the number of pole pairs.

question_text: The function of a constant speed drive (CSD) in an AC generating system is to :
option_a: drive the generator at a constant speed.
option_b: vary generator rpm in order to compensate for various AC loads.
option_c: directly maintain a constant proportion between the rpm of an engine and a generator.
option_d: vary the engine rpm (within limits) to compensate for various AC loads.
explanation: A Constant Speed Drive (CSD) takes the variable rotational speed of the aircraft engine and delivers a constant output speed to the AC generator. This ensures that the generator produces a stable frequency of 400 Hz regardless of engine power setting.

question_text: If two constant frequency AC generators are operating independently, then the phase relationship of each generator:
option_a: is unimportant.
option_c: must be 120° out of phase.
option_d: must be 240° out of phase.
explanation: When AC generators operate independently to supply separate electrical buses, their phase relationship is unimportant. Phase synchronization is only required when generators are connected in parallel to share a common busbar.

question_text: The purpose of a voltage regulator is to control the output voltage of the :
option_a: generator at varying loads and speeds.
option_c: generators at varying speeds and the batteries at varying loads.
option_d: output of the TRU.
explanation: A voltage regulator controls the output voltage of a generator by adjusting the strength of the exciter field current. This maintains a constant output voltage despite changes in generator rotational speed or variations in the connected electrical loads.

question_text: A 3 phase AC generator has 3 separate stator windings spaced at :
explanation: A three-phase AC generator has three separate stator windings physically and electrically spaced 120 degrees apart around the stator. This layout produces three separate voltages that are offset in phase by 120 degrees.

question_text: On the flight deck, an oil operated CSD unit is normally provided with means of monitoring the:
option_a: oil over-temperature and low oil pressure.
option_c: output speed and oil pressure.
option_d: low oil temperature and low oil quantity.
explanation: Because the Constant Speed Drive (CSD) relies on its own self-contained oil system for power transmission and cooling, it is critical to monitor its health. The flight deck is therefore equipped with indicators for CSD oil over-temperature and low oil pressure.

question_text: An AC generator driven by a CSD unit :
option_a: requires a voltage controller to maintain constant voltage under load.
option_b: does not need a voltage controller since the CSD will ensure constant voltage.
option_c: does not need a voltage controller since an AC generator voltage cannot alter under load.
option_d: requires a voltage controller to maintain constant frequency.
explanation: While a CSD ensures a constant rotor speed to maintain frequency, it does not regulate voltage. A separate voltage controller (GCU) is required to adjust excitation current and maintain a constant voltage under varying electrical loads.

question_text: Assuming a CSD fault is indicated, the CSD should be disconnected :
option_a: during engine operation only.
option_c: in accordance with the regulated voltage level of the AC generator.
option_d: on the ground only.
explanation: The CSD disconnect mechanism uses an electromagnetic solenoid to actuate a dog clutch. This disconnection must only be performed when the engine is operating, as the rotational torque of the shaft is required to disengage the clutch.

question_text: The measured output power components of a constant frequency AC system are :
option_a: kVA and kVAR.
option_c: volts and kilowatts.
option_d: amperes and kilowatts.
explanation: In AC circuits, total apparent power is measured in Volt-Amperes (VA or kVA), while reactive power is measured in Volt-Amperes Reactive (VAR or kVAR). Real power is measured in Watts (W or kW).

question_text: ""Frequency wild"" in relation to a AC generation system means the generator :
option_a: output frequency varies with engine speed.
option_c: voltage regulator is out of adjustment.
option_d: output frequency is too low.
explanation: A "frequency wild" AC generation system does not use a CSD, meaning the generator rotor speed varies directly with engine RPM. Consequently, the output frequency varies with engine speed, making it suitable only for non-frequency-sensitive loads like heating.

question_text: The function of a CSD in an AC generating system is to:
option_a: drive the generator at a constant speed.
option_b: vary the engine rpm (within limits) to compensate for various AC loads.
option_c: vary generator rpm in order to compensate for various AC loads.
option_d: directly maintain a constant proportion between the rpm of engine and generator.
explanation: A Constant Speed Drive (CSD) is a hydro-mechanical transmission designed to drive the generator at a constant rotational speed. This ensures the output frequency of the alternator remains constant, typically at 400 Hz.

question_text: The frequency of an AC generator is dependent on the :
option_a: number of pairs of poles and the speed of the moving part.
option_b: number of individual poles and the field strength.
option_c: field strength and the speed of the moving part.
option_d: number of individual poles only.
explanation: The frequency of alternating current produced by a generator is directly proportional to the rotational speed of the rotor (moving part) and the number of magnetic pole pairs. It is calculated as speed (RPM) multiplied by the number of pole pairs, divided by 60.

question_text: A Constant Speed Drive aims at ensuring
option_a: that the electric generator produces a constant frequency.
option_b: that the starter-motor maintains a constant RPM not withstanding the acceleration of the engine.
option_c: that the CSD remains at a constant RPM not withstanding the generator RPM
option_d: equal AC voltage from all generators.
explanation: The sole purpose of a Constant Speed Drive (CSD) is to maintain a constant rotational input to the generator, thereby ensuring the electrical output has a constant frequency. This frequency stability is critical for the proper operation of sensitive aircraft avionics.

question_text: A thermal circuit breaker:
option_a: protects the system in the event of overheating, even without exceeding the maximum permissible current.
option_b: is a protection system with a quick break capacity of about one hundredth of a second.
option_c: forbids any overcurrent.
option_d: can be reset without any danger even if the fault remains.
explanation: A thermal circuit breaker operates on the principle of heat generation caused by current flow. It protects the wiring and system from overheating, but it is not designed to trip instantaneously and must not be reset if a persistent fault exists.

question_text: In an aircraft electrical system where AC generators are not paralleled mounted, the changover relay allows :
option_a: power supply to the faulty AC generators busbar.
option_b: connection of the AC generator to its distribution busbar.
option_c: connection of the ground power truck to its distribution busbar.
option_d: connection of the Auxiliary Power Unit (APU) to its main busbar.
explanation: In non-paralleled electrical systems, a changeover relay (or bus tie contactor) automatically connects a healthy generator or alternative power source to the busbar of a failed generator. This ensures that essential services continue to receive power in the event of a generator failure.

question_text: Pulling the fire shutoff handle causes a number of devices to disconnect. In respect of the AC generator it can be said that the:
option_a: exciter control relay and the generator breaker open.
option_c: generator breaker opens.
option_d: exciter control relay, the generator breaker and the tie breaker open.
explanation: Pulling the fire shutoff handle isolates the engine by closing fuel, hydraulic, and pneumatic valves. Electrically, it opens the generator control relay (de-energizing the exciter field) and opens the generator breaker to isolate the alternator from the aircraft buses.

question_text: As regards three-phase AC generators, the following conditions must be met for paralleling AC generators:1. Equal voltage2. Equal current3. Equal frequencies4. Same phase rotation5. Voltages of same phaseThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is :
explanation: To safely connect two or more AC generators in parallel, they must have equal voltages, equal frequencies, the same phase rotation, and their voltages must be in phase (synchronous). Paralleling without meeting these conditions will cause large damaging currents to flow between generators.

question_text: A magnetic circuit-breaker is:
option_a: a protection system that has a quick tripping response.
option_b: permits an overcurrent limited in time.
option_c: can be reset without any danger even when fault remains.
option_d: is a system with a slow response time.
explanation: A magnetic circuit breaker uses an electromagnetic coil that reacts to the magnetic field generated by current flow. In the event of a short circuit or massive overcurrent, it trips almost instantaneously to prevent severe damage to the electrical system.

question_text: On detection of a persistent overvoltage fault on an AC generator connected to the aircraft AC busbars, the on-board protection device opens:
option_a: the exciter breaker and the generator breaker.
option_b: the exciter breaker, the generator breaker and tie breaker.
option_c: The generator breaker and tie breaker.
option_d: The generator breaker.
explanation: To protect the aircraft's electrical system from damage due to excessive voltage, the overvoltage protection circuit within the GCU will trip. This action opens both the generator exciter breaker (stopping voltage generation) and the generator breaker (isolating it from the busbar).

question_text: When a persistent top excitation limit fault on an AC generator connected to the mains with another AC generator, the overexcitation protection device opens:
option_a: the exciter breaker, the generator breaker and the tie breaker.
option_c: the exciter breaker and the generator breaker.
option_d: the generator breaker.
explanation: If a generator experiences a persistent top excitation fault while paralleled, it will export excessive reactive power. The protection system will open the exciter breaker, the generator breaker, and the tie breaker to fully isolate the malfunctioning unit and protect the shared bus.

question_text: When a persistent overexcitation fault is detected on only one AC generator, the protection device opens the :
option_a: exciter breaker and generator breaker.
option_b: exciter breaker, generator breaker and tie breaker.
option_c: tie breaker.
option_d: generator breaker and tie breaker.
explanation: When a persistent overexcitation fault is detected on a generator, it could lead to damaging overvoltages or excessive reactive load currents. The GCU protects the system by opening the exciter breaker (de-energizing the field) and opening the generator breaker.

question_text: When an underspeed fault is detected on an AC generator connected to the aircraft AC busbar, the protection device opens the:
option_a: generator breaker.
option_c: exciter breaker and generator breaker.
option_d: exciter breaker, generator breaker and tie breaker.
explanation: When a generator's rotational speed drops below the limits required to maintain the correct frequency, an underspeed sensor detects the fault. The GCU will then open the generator breaker to isolate the under-frequency power from the aircraft buses.

question_text: The services connected to a supply bus-bar are normally in:
option_a: parallel, so that isolating individual loads decreases the bus-bar current consumption.
option_b: series, so that isolating one load increases the bus-bar current consumption.
option_c: parallel, so that isolation of loads decreases the bus-bar voltage.
option_d: series, so that isolation of loads increases the bus-bar voltage.
explanation: Aircraft electrical services are connected to their supply busbars in parallel. This configuration ensures that all devices receive the same system voltage, and isolating or switching off individual loads reduces the total current drawn from the busbar.

question_text: To ensure correct load sharing between AC generators operating in parallel :
option_a: both real an reactive loads must be matched.
option_b: the matching of loads is unimportant.
option_c: only reactive loads need to be matched.
option_d: only real loads need to be matched.
explanation: For AC generators operating in parallel, both real load (measured in kW) and reactive load (measured in kVAR) must be balanced. Real load sharing is controlled by adjusting the CSD speed/torque, while reactive load sharing is managed by adjusting generator field excitation.

question_text: When operating two AC generators unparalleled, the phase relationship of each generator:
option_a: is unimportant.
option_c: must be in opposition.
option_d: must be 90° out of synchronisation.
explanation: When AC generators are operated in an unparallel configuration, they supply separate isolated electrical buses. Under these conditions, the phase relationship between the generators is unimportant since they are never electrically joined.

question_text: When AC generators are operated in paralllel, they must be of the same:
option_a: voltage and frequency.
option_c: voltage and amperage.
option_d: frequency and amperage.
explanation: Before connecting AC generators to a common busbar in parallel, they must be matched in both voltage and frequency. Mismatches will result in massive circulating currents between the alternators, causing damage and tripping the circuit breakers.

question_text: Real load sharing in a parallel AC system is achieved by :
option_a: automatic adjustment of the torque on each generator rotor via the CSD unit.
option_c: carefully selecting the number of loads on the bus-bars at any one time.
option_d: monitoring the kVAR of each generator/alternator.
explanation: Real load sharing (measured in kW) between paralleled AC generators is achieved by adjusting the mechanical torque applied to each generator rotor. The GCU commands fine adjustments to the governor of each CSD unit to balance this torque.

question_text: Real load sharing in a parallel AC system is achieved by :
option_a: adjusting the torque on each generator rotor via the CSD unit.
option_b: carefully secting the number of loads on the bus-bars at any one time.
option_c: controlling the generator field current.
option_d: monitoring the kVAR of each generator/alternator.
explanation: Real load sharing is managed by adjusting the mechanical torque delivered to each generator rotor through its Constant Speed Drive (CSD). This balances the active power (kilowatts) output among all paralleled alternators.

question_text: Load shedding means ..
option_a: Temporarily or permanent switching off of certain electric users to avoid overload of electric generators
option_b: To leave behind extra cargo if the centre of gravity moves outside limits
option_c: Reduction of airloads on the flaps by means of the flap load relief value
option_d: A procedure used in control systems to reduce the stick forces
explanation: Load shedding is an automated or manual emergency procedure where non-essential electrical services are disconnected. This reduces the total demand on the remaining healthy generators, preventing an overload and subsequent total system failure.

question_text: The speed of an asynchronous four-pole motor fed at a frequency of 400 Hertz is:
option_a: 12000 revolutions per minute.
option_c: 800 revolutions per minute.
option_d: 1600 revolutions per minute.
explanation: The synchronous speed of an AC motor is given by the formula Ns = (120 * f) / P. For a 4-pole motor running on a 400 Hz supply, the synchronous speed is (120 * 400) / 4 = 12000 RPM, with the actual asynchronous rotor speed being slightly less due to slip.

question_text: In an aeroplane utilising a constant frequency AC power supply, DC power is obtained from a :
option_a: Transformer Rectifier Unit.
option_c: 3 phase current transformer unit.
option_d: rotary converter.
explanation: On aircraft where the primary power generation is alternating current (AC), direct current (DC) is obtained using a Transformer Rectifier Unit (TRU). The TRU steps down the 115 V AC voltage and rectifies it to a standard 28 V DC output.

question_text: On an aeroplane utilising AC as primary power supplies, the batteries are charged in flight from :
option_a: a Transformer Rectifier Unit.
option_c: a DC transformer and rectifier.
option_d: the AC bus via current limiters.
explanation: Aircraft batteries require direct current (DC) for charging. In an AC-primary aircraft, the AC supply is directed through a Transformer Rectifier Unit (TRU) to produce 28 V DC, which is then used to charge the batteries.

question_text: In computer technology, an output peripheral is a:
option_a: screen unit
option_c: hard disk drive
option_d: diskette drive
explanation: In computer technology, an output peripheral is a device used to present or display processed data to the user. A screen unit (monitor) is a primary example of an output peripheral, whereas keyboards are input devices and hard disks are storage devices.

question_text: In computer technology, an input peripheral is a:
option_a: keyboard
option_c: hard disk drive
option_d: diskette drive
explanation: An input peripheral is a hardware device used to enter data or commands into a computer system. The keyboard is the primary input device, whereas screens are output devices and storage drives are for data retention.

question_text: In computer technology, a storage peripheral is a:
option_a: hard disk drive
option_c: key board
option_d: screen unit
explanation: A storage peripheral is a device designed to retain digital data even when the computer system is powered down. A hard disk drive is a typical storage peripheral, whereas keyboards and screens are input and output devices.

question_text: In computer technology, an EPROM is:1. a read-only memory2. a write memory3. erases its content when power supply is cut off4. keeps its content when power supply is cut offThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: An EPROM (Erasable Programmable Read-Only Memory) is a non-volatile memory chip, meaning it retains its content when the power supply is cut off. It functions as read-only memory during normal operation but can be erased under ultraviolet light and rewritten if needed.

question_text: (For this question use annex 021- 6660A)The logic symbol shown represents (assuming positive logic) :
option_a: an INVERT or NOT gate.
option_c: a NOR gate.
option_d: an EXCLUSIVE gate.
explanation: The logic symbol featuring a triangle with a small circle at the output represents an inverter or NOT gate. It performs logical negation, meaning the output is always the opposite state of the input.

question_text: Because of the input/output relationship of an AND gate, it is often referred to as the :
option_a: ""all or nothing"" gate.
option_c: ""state indicator"" gate.
option_d: ""inhibited"" or ""negated"" gate.
explanation: An AND gate requires all of its inputs to be in a high state (binary 1) to produce a high output. Because of this logical condition, it is often referred to as the "all or nothing" gate.

question_text: The function of a NOT logic gate within a circuit is to :
option_a: invert the input signal such that the output is always of the opposite state.
option_b: ensure the input signal is AC only.
option_c: ensure the input signal is DC only.
option_d: ensure the output signal is of the same state as the input signal.
explanation: The primary function of a NOT gate (also known as an inverter) is to invert the incoming binary signal. If the input is high (1), the output becomes low (0), and if the input is low, the output is high.

question_text: Because of the input/output relationship of an OR gate, it is often referred to as the :
option_a: ""any or all"" gate.
option_c: ""state indicator"" gate.
option_d: ""all or nothing"" gate.
explanation: An OR logic gate requires only one (or more) of its inputs to be in a high state (binary 1) to produce a high output. Because of this characteristic, it is often referred to as the "any or all" gate.

question_text: The wavelength of a radio transmitted on frequency 121.95 MHz is:
explanation: Wavelength is calculated as the speed of light divided by frequency. For a frequency of 121.95 MHz, the wavelength is approximately 300,000,000 divided by 121,950,000, which equals 2.46 metres.

question_text: For weather radar, the frequency 9375 MHz in X Band is preferable to C Band because:
option_a: It better detects clouds contour and range is greater with the same transmission power.
option_c: It is not absorbed by heavy precipitations.
option_d: It allows greater scanning rates.
explanation: X-band weather radar (9375 MHz) uses a shorter wavelength compared to C-band. This allows for better reflectivity from smaller water droplets, resulting in a more detailed cloud contour display and greater range for the same transmission power.

question_text: The wavelength of a non-directional beacon (NDB) at a frequency of 300 kHz is:
option_a: 1000 metres.
option_c: 10 metres.
option_d: 1 metre.
explanation: Using the wave propagation formula, where the speed of light is divided by frequency, the wavelength of an NDB operating at 300 kHz is calculated as 300,000,000 divided by 300,000, which equals 1000 metres.

question_text: The minimum airborne equipment required for operation of a the VHF direction finder is a:
option_a: VHF transmitter-receiver operating in the 118 MHz to 136 MHz range.
option_b: VHF compass operating in the 200 kHz to 1750 kHz range.
option_c: VHF receiver operating in the 118 MHz to 136 MHz range.
option_d: cathode-ray tube.
explanation: The VHF direction finder (VDF) is a ground-based service where the ground station calculates the aircraft's bearing from its radio transmissions. Consequently, the only airborne equipment required by the pilot is a standard VHF transmitter-receiver operating in the 118-136 MHz range.

question_text: The secondary Surveillance Radar (SSR) uses the following wavelengths:
option_a: decimetric.
option_c: hectometric.
option_d: myriametric.
explanation: Secondary Surveillance Radar (SSR) operates on frequencies of 1030 MHz (interrogation) and 1090 MHz (reply). These frequencies fall within the UHF band, which corresponds to decimetric wavelengths.

question_text: The airborne weather radar uses the following wavelengths:
option_a: centimetric.
option_c: hectometric.
option_d: myriametric.
explanation: Airborne weather radar operates in the X-band (approximately 9 GHz), which falls into the SHF radio frequency band. This high-frequency signal translates to centimetric wavelengths, which are ideal for reflecting off precipitation.

question_text: The VHF Omnirange (VOR) uses the following wavelengths:
option_a: metric.
option_c: decimetric.
option_d: centimetric.
explanation: VOR stations transmit in the Very High Frequency (VHF) band, specifically from 108.00 MHz to 117.975 MHz. Frequencies in this band have metric wavelengths, which propagate via line-of-sight.

question_text: The Instrument Landing System (ILS) uses the following wavelengths:
option_a: metric.
option_c: decimetric.
option_d: centimetric.
explanation: The Instrument Landing System (ILS) utilizes frequencies in the VHF band for the Localizer and the UHF band for the Glide Path. These allocations correspond to metric and decimetric bands, respectively, with ILS wavelengths categorized broadly as metric.

question_text: The Distance Measuring Equipment (DME) uses the following wavelengths:
option_a: decimetric.
option_c: metric.
option_d: centimetric.
explanation: Distance Measuring Equipment (DME) operates in the Ultra High Frequency (UHF) band, spanning from 960 MHz to 1215 MHz. These high frequencies correspond to decimetric wavelengths, which travel along line-of-sight paths.

question_text: The Fan Markers uses the following wavelengths:
option_a: metric.
option_c: hectometric.
option_d: myriametric.
explanation: Fan markers (marker beacons) transmit on a fixed frequency of 75 MHz. This frequency is within the VHF band, which corresponds to metric wavelengths.

question_text: The VHF direction finder uses the following wavelengths:
option_a: metric.
option_c: decimetric.
option_d: centimetric.
explanation: VHF direction finding (VDF) uses standard VHF communications frequencies between 118 MHz and 137 MHz. Signals in this frequency band propagate via line-of-sight using metric wavelengths.

question_text: The Microwave Landing System (MLS) uses the following wavelengths:
option_a: centimetric.
option_c: hectometric.
option_d: myriametric.
explanation: The Microwave Landing System (MLS) operates in the Super High Frequency (SHF) band between 5030 MHz and 5091 MHz. These high frequencies correspond to centimetric wavelengths, allowing for precise guidance signals.

question_text: The high Altitude Radio Altimeter uses the following wavelengths:
option_a: decimetric.
option_c: hectometric.
option_d: myriametric.
explanation: High-altitude radio altimeters typically operate in the UHF band (around 400 MHz). This frequency band utilizes decimetric wavelengths, which provide the range and penetration necessary for high-altitude measurements.

question_text: The Low Altitude Radio Altimeter uses the following wavelengths:
option_a: centimetric.
option_c: decimetric.
option_d: metric.
explanation: Low-altitude radio altimeters operate in the GHz range (usually around 4.2 to 4.4 GHz) in the SHF band. This allows the system to use centimetric wavelengths, providing the high resolution and accuracy required close to the ground.

question_text: The Automatic Direction Finder uses the following wavelengths:
option_a: hectometric or kilometric.
option_c: decimetric.
option_d: centimetric.
explanation: The Automatic Direction Finder (ADF) receives signals from ground-based Non-Directional Beacons (NDBs) operating in the LF and MF bands (200 kHz to 1750 kHz). These bands utilize hectometric or kilometric wavelengths.

question_text: In the response curve of an amplifier, the bandwidth is:
option_a: The frequency band corresponding to maximum gain less 3 decibels.
option_b: The frequency band corresponding to maximum gain.
option_c: The frequency band corresponding to maximum gain less 20 decibels.
option_d: The frequency band corresponding to maximum gain, increased by 10 kHz at each end.
explanation: The bandwidth of an amplifier is defined as the range of frequencies over which the output power does not drop below 50% of its maximum value. This power drop corresponds to a reduction in voltage gain of 3 decibels (-3 dB).

question_text: In aviation, the reflection on ionosphere layers phenomenon is used in the following frequencies:
option_a: HF
option_c: UHF
option_d: VLF
explanation: HF (High Frequency) signals, operating between 3 MHz and 30 MHz, are reflected by the ionospheric layers, producing "sky waves". This reflection allows for long-distance over-the-horizon communications.

question_text: Skip distance is the:
option_a: range from the transmitter to the first sky wave
option_c: wavelength distance of a certain frequency
option_d: thickness of the ionosphere
explanation: Skip distance is the geographical distance between the transmitter and the point where the first reflected sky wave returns to the Earth's surface. Within this area, there is a skip zone where the signal cannot be received.

question_text: A radio signal looses strength as range from the transmitter increases, this is called :
option_a: attenuation
option_c: propagation
option_d: ducting
explanation: Attenuation is the term used to describe the gradual loss of signal strength or amplitude as a radio wave propagates away from the transmitter. It is caused by wave spreading, atmospheric absorption, and ground losses.

question_text: The skip zone of HF-transmission will increase when the following change in circumstance occurs :
option_a: Higher frequency and higher position of the reflecting ionospheric layer
option_b: Lower frequency ang higher position of the reflecting ionospheric layer
option_c: Higher frequency and lower position of the reflecting ionospheric layer
option_d: Lower frequency and lower position of the reflecting ionospheric layer
explanation: The skip zone increases when the frequency is higher (causing less refraction, so the wave penetrates deeper or passes through lower layers) and when the reflecting ionospheric layer is higher. Both factors cause the sky wave to return to Earth further away from the transmitter.

question_text: In the propagation of MF waves, the phenomenon of FADING is particularly found :
option_a: at night, due to the combination of the sky and ground waves.
option_b: by day, due to the combination of sky and ground waves.
option_c: at night and when raining.
option_d: by day and when raining.
explanation: Fading is a fluctuation in signal strength at the receiver caused by phase interference. It is most common at night when the ionosphere reflects MF sky waves, which then combine out of phase with the ground wave.

question_text: The positions of the intake and exhaust valve at the end of the power stroke are :
option_a: intake valve closed and exhaust valve open.
option_c: both valves closed.
option_d: exhaust valve closed and intake valve open.
explanation: At the end of the power (expansion) stroke, the piston approaches Bottom Dead Centre (BDC) and the combustion gas pressure must be vented. Consequently, the exhaust valve begins to open while the intake valve remains closed to prepare for the exhaust stroke.

question_text: The useful work area in an ideal Otto engine indicator diagram is enclosed by the following gas state change lines
option_a: 2 adiabatic and 2 isochoric lines.
option_c: 2 adiabatic and 2 isobaric lines.
option_d: 2 adiabatic, 1 isochoric and 1 isobaric lines.
explanation: The thermodynamic cycle of an ideal four-stroke Otto engine is represented on a P-V indicator diagram. The area enclosing the useful work is bounded by two adiabatic lines representing compression and expansion, and two isochoric lines representing constant-volume heat addition and rejection.

question_text: The correct formula to calculate the multi-cylinder engine displacement is :
option_a: piston area * piston stroke * number of cylinders
option_c: cylinder volume * number of cylinders
option_d: cylinder length * cylinder diameter
explanation: Engine displacement is the total volume swept by all pistons in the cylinders. It is calculated by multiplying the cross-sectional area of one piston by the length of its stroke, and then multiplying by the total number of cylinders.

question_text: In most cases aeroplane piston engines are short stroke engines. This permits a :
option_a: lighter construction.
option_c: better piston cooling.
option_d: cheaper construction
explanation: A short-stroke (or oversquare) engine has a cylinder bore diameter that is larger than the stroke length. This design keeps the height and width of the engine compact, allowing for a lighter crankcase and cylinder construction.

question_text: The working cycle of a four-stroke engine is :
option_a: induction, compression, power, exhaust.
option_c: compression induction, power, exhaust.
option_d: induction, compression, expansion, power.
explanation: The thermodynamic and mechanical cycle of a four-stroke internal combustion engine consists of four distinct stages. These strokes always occur in the sequence of induction (intake), compression, power (combustion/expansion), and exhaust.

question_text: The crank assembly consists of
option_a: crankshaft, connecting rods and pistons.
option_b: propeller, crankshaft, pistons and connecting rods.
option_c: Crankcase, crankshaft, connecting rods and pistons.
option_d: crankshaft, camshaft, valves, valve springs and push rods.
explanation: The crank assembly (or reciprocating assembly) converts the linear motion of the pistons into rotational motion. It is composed of the crankshaft, the connecting rods, and the pistons.

question_text: The ignition occurs in each cylinder of an four-stroke engine (TDC = Top Dead Center)
option_a: before TDC at each second crankshaft revolution.
option_b: before TDC at each crankshaft revolution.
option_c: behind TDC at each crankshaft revolution.
option_d: behind TDC at each second crankshaft revolution.
explanation: In a four-stroke engine, a complete cycle requires two full crankshaft revolutions. The spark ignition must occur just before Top Dead Centre (TDC) at the end of the compression stroke, which happens once every second revolution.

question_text: The power output of a piston engine can be calculated by :
option_a: Torque times RPM.
option_c: Force times distance.
option_d: Pressure times arm.
explanation: Mechanical power output is defined as the rate of doing work and is mathematically calculated by multiplying torque by rotational speed (RPM). For an aircraft engine, this determines the shaft power delivered to the propeller.

question_text: The power of a piston engine which will be measured by using a friction brake is :
option_a: Brake horse power.
option_c: Heat loss power.
option_d: Indicated horse power.
explanation: Brake Horsepower (BHP) is the actual usable power delivered by the engine crankshaft to the propeller. It is measured experimentally by applying a braking force to the shaft using a dynamometer or friction brake.

question_text: The torque of an aeroplane engine can be measured at the:
option_a: gear box which is located between the engine and the propeller.
option_c: accessory gear box.
option_d: camshaft.
explanation: Engine torque is typically measured using sensors located in the reduction gearbox housing situated between the engine crankshaft and the propeller shaft. The reaction torque on the ring gear is measured to calculate the output torque.

question_text: On four-stroke piston engines, the theoretical valve and ignition settings are readjusted in order to increase the:
option_a: overall efficiency
option_c: piston displacement
option_d: engine r.p.m.
explanation: In practice, valves do not open and close exactly at dead centres, and ignition occurs early to allow time for flame propagation. Readjusting these valve and ignition timings (lead, lag, overlap) is done to maximize volumetric efficiency and overall engine power.

question_text: In a four-stroke piston engine, the only ""driving"" stroke is :
option_a: firing-expansion
option_c: compression
option_d: exhaust
explanation: In a four-stroke engine, three of the strokes (induction, compression, and exhaust) consume energy stored in the flywheel or other pistons. The firing-expansion (power) stroke is the only stroke that generates positive power to drive the crankshaft.

question_text: A piston engine compression ratio is the ratio of the :
option_a: total volume to the clearance volume.
option_b: clearance volume to the swept volume.
option_c: total volume to the swept volume.
option_d: swept volume to the clearance volume.
explanation: The compression ratio is the volume of the cylinder when the piston is at BDC (total volume) compared to the volume left when the piston is at TDC (clearance volume). It is a key factor in determining the engine's thermodynamic efficiency.

question_text: The compression ratio of a piston engine is the ratio of the:
option_a: volume of the cylinder with the piston at bottom dead centre to that with the piston at top dead centre.
option_b: diameter of the bore to the piston stroke.
option_c: area of the piston to the cylinder volume.
option_d: weight of the air induced to its weight after compression.
explanation: The compression ratio is defined as the ratio of the maximum cylinder volume (with the piston at bottom dead centre) to the minimum cylinder volume (with the piston at top dead centre). A higher ratio generally increases engine efficiency but increases the risk of detonation.

question_text: The part of a piston engine that transforms reciprocating movement into rotary motion is termed the :
option_a: crankshaft
option_c: camshaft
option_d: reduction gear
explanation: The crankshaft is the primary engine component designed to convert the linear reciprocating motion of the pistons, transmitted via the connecting rods, into useful rotary motion to drive the propeller.

question_text: The reading on the oil pressure gauge is the:
option_a: pressure of the oil on the outlet side of the pressure pump.
option_b: difference between the pressure pump pressure and the scavenge pump pressure.
option_c: pressure in the oil tank reservoir.
option_d: pressure of the oil on the inlet side of the pressure pump.
explanation: The oil pressure gauge measures the pressure of the lubricating oil immediately after it leaves the high-pressure outlet of the oil pump. This ensures the pilot is monitoring the actual pressure of the oil entering the engine bearings.

question_text: For a given type of oil, the oil viscosity depends on the:
option_a: oil temperature.
option_c: oil pressure.
option_d: quantity of oil.
explanation: The viscosity of an engine lubricating oil (its resistance to flow) is highly dependent on its temperature. As the oil temperature increases, its viscosity decreases, making it thinner and potentially reducing its load-bearing capability.

question_text: For internal cooling,reciprocating engines are especially dependent on:
option_a: the circulation of lubricating oil
option_c: a properly functioning thermostat
option_d: a lean fuel/air mixture
explanation: In addition to external air cooling, aircraft reciprocating engines rely heavily on the circulation of lubricating oil to carry heat away from high-stress internal components like bearings, pistons, and cylinder walls.

question_text: In addition to the fire hazard introduced, excessive priming should be avoided because :
option_a: it washes the lubricant of cylinder walls
option_c: it drains the carburettor float chamber
option_d: the gasoline dilutes the oil and necessitates changing oil
explanation: Priming injects raw fuel directly into the cylinders or intake manifold to assist in cold starts. Excessive priming can wash the protective lubricating oil film off the cylinder walls, leading to increased piston ring wear and a risk of fire in the intake system.

question_text: The oil system for a piston engine incorporates an oil cooler that is fitted :
option_a: in the return line to the oil tank after the oil has passed through the scavenge pump
option_b: between the oil tank and the pressure pump
option_c: after the pressure pump but before the oil passes through the engine
option_d: after the oil has passed through the engine and before it enters the sump
explanation: In a dry-sump oil system, the oil cooler is typically installed in the return line to the oil reservoir. This ensures that the hot oil drawn from the engine sump by the scavenge pump is cooled before it is stored in the oil tank.

question_text: Low oil pressure is sometimes the result of a
option_a: worn oil pump
option_c: restricted oil passage
option_d: too small scavenger pump.
explanation: Low oil pressure can be caused by mechanical wear in the oil pump gears, which prevents the pump from generating the required pressure. Other common causes include low oil level, high oil temperature (low viscosity), or a faulty pressure relief valve.

question_text: The purpose of a distributor in an ignition system is to distribute:
option_a: secondary current to the sparking plugs.
option_c: secondary current to the condenser.
option_d: primary current to the sparking plugs.
explanation: The distributor is a high-voltage rotary switch within the magneto system. Its function is to direct the high-tension secondary current from the coil to the individual spark plugs in the correct firing sequence.

question_text: The very rapid magnetic field changes (flux) around the primary coil in a magneto are accomplished by the:
option_a: contact breaker points opening.
option_b: distributor arm aligning with one of the high tension segments.
option_c: contact breaker points closing.
option_d: rotor turning past the position of maximum flux in the armature.
explanation: The high-voltage spark is produced by electromagnetic induction. When the contact breaker points open, the primary current is abruptly stopped, causing the primary magnetic field to collapse rapidly, which induces a high voltage in the secondary coil.

question_text: If the ground wire between the magnetos and the ignition switch becomes disconnected the most noticeable result will be that:
option_a: the engine cannot be shut down by turning the ignition switch to the ""OFF"" position
option_b: a still operating engine will run down
option_c: the engine cannot be started with the ignition switch in the ""ON"" position
option_d: the power developed by the engine will be strongly reduced
explanation: The magneto ignition system is shut down by grounding the primary circuit to the airframe through a ground wire (P-lead). If this ground wire is disconnected or broken, the magneto remains permanently "hot," meaning the engine cannot be shut down by turning the switch to "OFF."

question_text: The purpose of an ignition switch is to :
option_a: control the primary circuit of the magneto
option_b: connect the secondary coil to the distributor
option_c: connect the battery to the magneto
option_d: connect the contact breaker and condenser in series with the primary coil
explanation: The cockpit ignition switch controls the magneto by grounding or ungrounding its primary electrical circuit. When the switch is set to "OFF," the primary coil is connected to ground, preventing the contact points from interrupting current and stopping the spark.

question_text: Under normal running conditions a magneto draws primary current :
option_a: from a self-contained electro-magnetic induction system.
option_c: directly from the aircraft batteries.
option_d: from the aircraft batteries via an inverter.
explanation: A magneto is an independent, engine-driven generator that requires no battery power. It generates its own alternating primary current via electromagnetic induction as permanent magnets rotate past an armature.

question_text: Ignition systems of piston engines are :
option_a: independant from the electrical system of the aircraft.
option_c: dependant on the DC-Generator.
option_d: dependant on the AC-Generator.
explanation: Aircraft magneto ignition systems are completely self-contained and independent of the main aircraft electrical system (generator and battery). This design ensures that the engine will continue to run normally even in the event of a total aircraft electrical failure.

question_text: Prolonged running at low rpm may have an adverse effect on the efficiency of the:
option_a: sparking plugs.
option_c: oil pump.
option_d: fuel filter.
explanation: Operating a piston engine at low RPM for extended periods can lead to incomplete combustion and low cylinder temperatures. This causes carbon and lead deposits to accumulate on the spark plugs, resulting in plug fouling and misfires.

question_text: An aircraft magneto is switched off by
option_a: grounding the primary circuit
option_c: opening the secondary circuit
option_d: grounding the secondary circuit.
explanation: An aircraft magneto is switched off by grounding the primary circuit. Connecting the primary winding to the airframe structure (ground) prevents the contact breaker points from interrupting the current flow, which stops the induction of high voltage in the secondary circuit.

question_text: An impulse magneto coupling
option_a: gives a retarded spark at starting
option_b: reduces magneto speed during engine warm-up
option_c: advances ignition timing and gives a hotter spark at starting
option_d: gives an automatic spark increase during high speed operation.
explanation: An impulse coupling is a spring-loaded mechanical link between the engine drive and the magneto shaft. During startup, it temporarily holds back the magneto rotor and then releases it rapidly, producing a hot, retarded spark to prevent engine kickback and ensure reliable ignition at low starting RPM.

question_text: If an engine fails to stop with the magneto switch in OFF position, the cause may be :
option_a: excessive carbon formation in cylinder head.
option_c: defective condenser
option_d: fouled spark plugs
explanation: If an engine fails to stop with the magneto switch in the OFF position, it may be due to "dieseling" or auto-ignition caused by local hot spots in the combustion chamber. This is often the result of excessive carbon deposits in the cylinder head that remain glowing hot.

question_text: If the ground wire between the magneto and the ignition switch becomes disconnected, the most noticeable result will be that the engine
option_a: cannot be shut down by turning the switch to the OFF position.
option_b: will not operate at the left magneto
option_c: will not operate at the right magneto
option_d: cannot be started with the switch in the ON position
explanation: The ground wire (P-lead) is the electrical path used to shut down the magneto by grounding its primary circuit. If this wire is broken or disconnected, the magneto cannot be grounded, meaning the engine will continue to run even when the ignition switch is turned to the "OFF" position.

question_text: An impulse coupling used on a magneto for a piston engine is for
option_a: providing a retarded spark for engine starting.
option_c: quick removal and installation
option_d: absorbing starting loads
explanation: At low cranking speeds, the magneto does not spin fast enough to produce a strong spark, and early spark timing could cause the engine to kick back. The impulse coupling addresses this by delaying (retarding) the spark and spinning the magneto rotor rapidly at the moment of firing to provide a hot start spark.

question_text: In a piston engine, magnetos are used to produce the spark which ignites the fuel/ air mixture. The operating principle of magnetos consists in :
option_a: breaking the primary current in order to induce a low amp high volt current which is distributed to the spark plugs.
option_b: obtaining a high amp low volt current in order to generate the spark.
option_c: accumulating in a condenser a low volt current from the battery, reconstitute it as high voltage current at the moment the spark is generated.
option_d: creating a brief high intensity magnetic field which will be sent through the distributor at the appropriate time.
explanation: A magneto generates high voltage using electromagnetic induction. When the contact breaker points open, they abruptly break the primary current, which causes the primary magnetic field to collapse rapidly and induce a high-voltage, low-amperage current in the secondary coil to fire the spark plugs.

question_text: When the magneto selector switch is set to ""OFF"" position, the piston engine continues to run normally.The most probable cause of this failure is that:
option_a: On a magneto, a grounding wire is broken.
option_b: There is a carbon deposit on the spark plugs electrodes.
option_c: A wire from the magneto is in contact with a metallic part of the engine.
option_d: There are local hot points in the engine (probably due to overheating of the cylinder heads).
explanation: The most common mechanical cause for an engine continuing to run when switched to "OFF" is a broken or disconnected grounding wire (P-lead) on one of the magnetos. Because the primary circuit cannot be grounded to the airframe, the magneto remains active or "hot."

question_text: On modern carburettors, the variations of mixture ratios are obtained by the adjustment of :
option_a: fuel flow.
option_c: fuel flow and air flow.
option_d: fuel flow, air flow and temperature.
explanation: Modern aircraft float-type carburettors adjust the fuel/air mixture ratio by regulating the fuel flow through the metering jets rather than altering the airflow. This is accomplished using a pilot-controlled mixture lever that adjusts the needle valve or fuel passage size.

question_text: A fuel strainer when fitted to a carburettor will be positioned :
option_a: upstream of the needle valve.
option_b: between the needle valve and the metering jet.
option_c: between the metering jet and the discharge nozzle.
option_d: downstream of th discharge nozzle.
explanation: To prevent debris from clogging the precise internal orifices of the carburettor, a fuel strainer or filter is positioned upstream of the needle valve at the inlet to the float chamber. This ensures all entering fuel is filtered before passing through the metering system.

question_text: The purpose of the venturi in a carburettor is to:
option_a: create the depression necessary to cause fuel to flow through the carburettor jets.
option_b: prevent enrichment of the mixture due to high air velocity through the carburettor.
option_c: ensure complete atomisation of the fuel before entering the induction system.
option_d: create a rise in pressure at the throat before the mixture enters the induction system.
explanation: The venturi is a restriction in the carburettor barrel that increases air velocity and, in accordance with Bernoulli's principle, decreases air pressure at the throat. This localized pressure drop (depression) sucks fuel from the main discharge nozzle into the passing airflow.

question_text: In which sections of the carburettor would icing most likely occur?
option_a: venturi and the throttle valve
option_b: float chamber and fuel inlet filter
option_c: accelerator pump and main metering jet
option_d: main air bleed and main discharge nozzle
explanation: Carburettor icing is most likely to occur in the venturi throat and around the throttle valve. The combined effects of fuel vaporization cooling and the pressure drop across the throttle valve can cause temperature drops of up to 30 degrees Celsius, freezing atmospheric moisture.

question_text: The operating principle of float-type carburettors is based on the:
option_a: difference in air pressure at the venturi throat and the air inlet
option_b: automatic metering of air at the venturi as the aircraft gains altitude
option_c: increase in air velocity in the throat of a venturi causing an increase in air pressure
option_d: measurement of the fuel flow into the induction system
explanation: Float-type carburettors rely on the difference in air pressure between the air inlet (at atmospheric pressure) and the lower pressure at the venturi throat. This pressure differential draws fuel out of the float chamber and sprays it into the intake air.

question_text: In an engine equipped with a float-type carburettor, the low temperature that causes carburettor ice is normally the result of:
option_a: vaporization of fuel and expansion of the air in the carburettor
option_b: freezing temperature of the air entering the carburettor
option_c: compression of air at the carburettor venturi
option_d: low volatility of aviation fuel
explanation: The severe temperature drop inside a carburettor is primarily caused by two thermodynamic processes: the vaporization of fuel (latent heat of vaporization) and the expansion of air as it passes through the venturi and past the throttle valve. These cooling processes can freeze moisture even on warm days.

question_text: Which statement is true concerning the effect of the application of carburettor heat?
option_a: it reduces the density of air entering the carburettor, thus enriching the fuel/air mixture
option_b: it reduces the volume of air entering the carburettor,thus leaning the fuel/air mixture
option_c: it reduces the density of air entering the carburettor, thus leaning the fuel/air mixture
option_d: it reduces the volume of air entering the carburettor,thus enriching the fuel/air mixture
explanation: Applying carburettor heat routes unfiltered air warmed by the exhaust shroud into the intake. Because warm air is less dense than cold air, the mass of air entering the engine decreases, which enriches the fuel/air mixture unless the mixture control is adjusted.

question_text: Vapour lock is :
option_a: vaporizing of fuel prior to reaching the carburettor
option_b: the formation of water vapour in a fuel system
option_c: vaporizing of fuel in the carburettor
option_d: the inability of a fuel to vaporize in the carburettor
explanation: Vapour lock is a condition where fuel in the supply lines vaporizes due to excessive heat or low atmospheric pressure, forming bubbles or vapor pockets. These vapor locks block the flow of liquid fuel to the carburettor, causing engine roughness or complete flameout.

question_text: With respect to a piston engined aircraft, ice in the carburettor :
option_a: may form at OAT's higher than +10°C.
option_b: will only form at OAT's below +10°C.
option_c: will only form at outside air temperatures (OAT's) below the freezing point of water.
option_d: will only form at OAT's below the freezing point of fuel.
explanation: Because the temperature drop within a carburettor can be as much as 30 degrees Celsius, carburettor ice can easily form at outside air temperatures (OAT) well above freezing, typically up to +25 degrees Celsius, especially in high relative humidity.

question_text: To ensure that the fuel flow is kept directly proportional to the volume of air flowing through the choke, thus preventing the main jet supplying excessive fuel as engine speed is increased, a carburettor is fitted with :
option_a: a diffuser
option_c: an accelerator pump
option_d: a mixture control
explanation: As engine speed increases, the air velocity through the venturi increases, causing the carburettor to naturally supply an excessively rich mixture. To prevent this, a diffuser introduces air bubbles into the fuel line, restricting fuel flow and maintaining a constant fuel/air ratio.

question_text: Spark timing is related to engine speed in the way that the:
option_a: faster the engine functions, the more the spark is advanced
option_b: slower the engine functions, the more the spark is advanced
option_c: faster the engine functions, the further past TDC the spark occurs
option_d: faster the engine functions, the more retarded the spark is.
explanation: As engine RPM increases, the pistons travel faster, but the time required for the fuel/air mixture to burn remains relatively constant. To ensure peak combustion pressure occurs at the optimum crankshaft angle, the spark timing must be advanced as engine speed increases.

question_text: ""Vapor lock"" is the phenomenon by which:
option_a: heat produces vapour plugs in the fuel line.
option_b: water vapour plugs are formed in the intake fuel line following the condensation of water in fuel tanks which have not been drained for sometime.
option_c: abrupt and abnormal enrichment of the fuel/air mixture following an inappropriate use of carburettor heat.
option_d: burnt gas plugs forming and remaining in the exhaust manifold following an overheat and thereby disturbing the exhaust.
explanation: Vapour lock occurs when high temperatures in the engine compartment or fuel lines cause the aviation fuel to boil and vaporize before reaching the fuel metering system. These vapor bubbles disrupt the fuel pump's ability to deliver liquid fuel, starving the engine.

question_text: The power of a piston engine decreases during climb with a constant power lever setting, because of the decreasing :
option_a: air density.
option_c: humidity.
option_d: temperature.
explanation: In a normally aspirated engine, the power output is directly dependent on the mass of air drawn into the cylinders. As the aircraft climbs, the atmospheric pressure and air density decrease, which reduces the mass of the intake charge and decreases engine power.

question_text: The conditions under which you obtain the highest engine power are :
option_a: cold and dry air at high pressure.
option_b: warm and humid air at low pressure.
option_c: cold and humid air at high pressure.
option_d: warm and dry air at high pressure.
explanation: An internal combustion engine produces maximum power when it can burn the greatest mass of fuel and air. This condition is achieved when the intake air is cold, dry, and at high pressure, as these environmental factors maximize air density.

question_text: The power output of a normally aspirated piston engine increases with increasing altitude at constant Manifold Air Pressure (MAP) and RPM because of the :
option_a: lower back pressure.
option_b: lower losses during the gas change.
option_c: lower friction losses.
option_d: leaner mixture at higher altitudes.
explanation: If manifold air pressure (MAP) and RPM are held constant during a climb (which requires a supercharged engine), engine power actually increases slightly. This is because the surrounding atmospheric pressure decreases, reducing the exhaust backpressure and improving scavenging efficiency.

question_text: During climb with constant Manifold Air Pressure (MAP) and RPM indication and constant mixture setting, the power output of a piston engine :
option_a: increases.
option_c: only stays constant if the speed control lever is pushed forward.
option_d: stays constant.
explanation: If manifold air pressure (MAP) and RPM are held constant during a climb, the power output of the engine increases. The primary reason is the decrease in ambient pressure, which reduces exhaust backpressure, allowing the cylinders to exhaust burnt gases more efficiently.

question_text: The global output of a piston engine is of:(global output = Thermal energy corresponding to the available shaft/power over the total thermal energy produced).
explanation: Piston engines are relatively inefficient heat engines. Only about 30% (a ratio of 0.30) of the total heat energy released by the combustion of fuel is converted into useful mechanical shaft power, with the remaining 70% lost to the exhaust, cooling, and friction.

question_text: A turbocharger system is normally driven by:
option_a: the exhaust system.
option_c: an hydraulic motor.
option_d: an electrically activated hydraulically powered clutch.
explanation: A turbocharger is a supercharging device driven entirely by the engine's high-energy exhaust gas flow. The exhaust gases pass through a turbine wheel, which rotates a shaft connected directly to the compressor impeller.

question_text: A turbocharger consists of a :
option_a: compressor and turbine mounted on a common shaft.
option_b: compressor and turbine on individual shafts.
option_c: compressor driving a turbine via a reduction gear.
option_d: turbine driving a compressor via a reduction gear.
explanation: A turbocharger is comprised of a centrifugal compressor impeller and an exhaust gas turbine wheel mounted on opposite ends of a common shaft. This design allows the turbine to drive the compressor directly without the need for complex mechanical gears.

question_text: The air in a piston engine turbo-supercharger centrifugal compressor :
option_a: enters the eye of the impeller and leaves at a tangent to the periphery.
option_b: enters via the diffuser and is fed to the impeller at the optimum angle of attack.
option_c: enters at the periphery and leaves via the eye of the impeller.
option_d: enters at a tangent to the rotor and leaves via the stator.
explanation: In a centrifugal compressor, air enters axially near the center (the eye) of the rotating impeller. The impeller flings the air outward radially, accelerating it toward the outer periphery where a diffuser converts this velocity energy into static pressure.

question_text: In a piston engine, turbocharger boost pressure may be monitored by :
option_a: a manifold pressure gauge only.
option_b: a cylinder head temperature gauge (CHT), a manifold pressure gauge, and engine rpm readings.
option_c: both a CHT gauge and manifold pressure gauge.
option_d: both engine rpm readings and a manifold pressure gauge.
explanation: The primary instrument used to monitor the boost pressure supplied to the engine by a turbocharger is the manifold pressure gauge. This gauge displays the absolute pressure of the fuel/air mixture inside the engine intake manifold, measured in inches of mercury.

question_text: The primary purpose of a supercharger is to :
option_a: maintain power at altitude
option_b: increase quantity of fuel at metering jet
option_c: provide leaner mixtures at altitudes below 5000 ft
option_d: provide a richer mixture at high altitudes
explanation: The primary purpose of a supercharger or turbocharger is to compress the intake air, maintaining sea-level manifold pressure and engine power output as the aircraft climbs into less dense air at higher altitudes.

question_text: The kind of compressor normally used as a supercharger is :
option_a: a radial compressor.
option_c: a hybrid compressor.
option_d: a piston compressor.
explanation: The compressor type used in aircraft piston engine supercharging systems is almost exclusively a centrifugal (or radial) compressor. This type of compressor is lightweight, compact, and highly efficient at the high rotational speeds of engine drives.

question_text: What can be the consequence during a descent with a fully open throttle if the waste gate is seized ?
option_a: The manifold air pressure (MAP) value may exceed the maximum allowed value.
option_b: The power of the motor will decrease.
option_c: The turbine shaft will break.
option_d: The turbine blades will separate.
explanation: If the turbocharger wastegate becomes seized in the closed or partially closed position, it cannot regulate the exhaust flow through the turbine. During a descent into denser air with a high throttle setting, this will cause the compressor to overboost the engine, potentially exceeding the maximum safe manifold air pressure (MAP).

question_text: One of the advantages of a turbosupercharger is that :
option_a: it uses the exhaust gas energy which normally is lost.
option_b: it has a better propulsive efficiency.
option_c: there is no torsion at the crankshaft.
option_d: there is no danger of knocking.
explanation: Unlike a mechanically driven supercharger which drains power from the engine crankshaft, a turbocharger is driven by the energy of the exhaust gases. It recovers this thermal and kinetic energy, which would otherwise be lost to the atmosphere, to compress the intake air.

question_text: The octane rating of a fuel characterises the :
option_a: the anti-knock capability
option_c: quantity of heat generated by its combustion
option_d: fuel electrical conductivity
explanation: The octane rating of an aviation gasoline is a measure of its chemical resistance to detonation or "knocking" during combustion. A higher octane rating indicates a fuel can withstand higher temperatures and pressures before igniting prematurely.

question_text: Fuel stored in aircraft tanks will accumulate moisture. The most practical way to minimize this when an aircraft is used every day or so is to :
option_a: keep tanks topped off when the aircraft is not in use
option_b: drain tanks at end of each day's flight
option_c: use only high octane gasoline
option_d: keep tank vents plugged and filler cap tight
explanation: Water vapor in the unfilled portion of aircraft fuel tanks will condense into liquid water as ambient temperatures drop. To minimize this condensation, the fuel tanks should be filled to capacity (topped off) immediately after flight, leaving no space for moist air.

question_text: The octane rating of a fuel and compression ratio of a piston engine have which of the following relations?
option_a: the higher the octane rating is, the higher the possible compression ratio is
option_b: the lower the octane rating is, the higher the possible compression ratio is
option_c: the higher the octane rating is, the lower the possible compression ratio is.
option_d: compression ratio is independent of the octane rating.
explanation: An engine with a higher compression ratio subjects the fuel/air mixture to greater pressures and temperatures prior to ignition, increasing the risk of detonation. Therefore, engines with higher compression ratios require fuel with a higher octane rating to prevent knock.

question_text: A piston engine may use a fuel of a different grade than the recommended:
option_a: provided that the grade is higher
option_b: provided that the grade is lower
option_c: never
option_d: provided that it is an aeronautical petrol
explanation: If the recommended grade of aviation fuel is unavailable, a higher-grade fuel may be used as a temporary substitute because it offers superior detonation resistance. However, a lower-grade fuel must never be used as it will lead to severe detonation and engine damage.

question_text: A rich mixture setting has to be used during climb segments. This results in a
option_a: lower cylinder head temperature.
option_c: slight loss of power.
option_d: higher torque.
explanation: During high-power climb segments, a rich fuel/air mixture is commanded to provide internal cooling for the cylinders. The excess fuel that does not burn absorbs heat as it vaporizes, which lowers the cylinder head temperature (CHT) and prevents overheating.

question_text: Max. Exhaust Gas Temperature is theoretically associated with :
option_a: Mass ratio of 1/15.
option_c: Full rich setting.
option_d: Mixture ratio very close to idle cut-out.
explanation: Maximum Exhaust Gas Temperature (EGT) is achieved when the fuel/air mixture ratio is at its stoichiometric value, which is approximately 1:15 by weight. At this ratio, there is just enough oxygen to burn all the fuel completely, releasing the maximum amount of heat.

question_text: For piston engines, mixture ratio is the ratio between the :
option_a: mass of fuel and mass of air entering the cylinder.
option_b: volume of fuel and volume of air entering the cylinder.
option_c: volume of fuel and volume of air entering the carburettor.
option_d: mass of fuel and volume of air entering the carburettor.
explanation: In piston engines, the mixture ratio is defined as the ratio between the mass of fuel and the mass of air entering the cylinder. Measuring by mass is essential because the density of air changes significantly with pressure and temperature.

question_text: Specific fuel consumption is defined as the :
option_a: mass of fuel required to produce unit power for unit time.
option_b: designed fuel consumption for a given rpm.
option_c: quantity of fuel required to run the engine for one minute at maximum operating conditions.
option_d: maximum fuel consumption of the aircraft.
explanation: Specific Fuel Consumption (SFC) is a measure of an engine's fuel efficiency. It is defined as the mass of fuel consumed per hour to produce a unit of power (such as Brake Horsepower or Kilowatts).

question_text: In a piston engine, the purpose of an altitude mixture control is to :
option_a: correct for variations in the fuel/air ratio due to decreased air density at altitude.
option_b: prevent a weak cut when the throttle is opened rapidly at altitude.
option_c: weaken the mixture strength because of reduced exhaust back pressure at altitude.
option_d: enrich the mixture strength due to decreased air density at altitude.
explanation: As an aircraft climbs, air density decreases, meaning there is less oxygen by weight in a given volume of air. The altitude mixture control allows the pilot or an automatic system to decrease the fuel flow, correcting the fuel/air ratio to prevent the mixture from becoming excessively rich.

question_text: The mixture control for a carburettor achieves its control by:
option_a: varying the fuel supply to the main discharge tube.
option_b: moving the butterfly valve through a separate linkage to the main throttle control.
option_c: altering the depression on the main discharge tube.
option_d: varying the air supply to the main discharge tube.
explanation: The mixture control in a float-type carburettor adjusts the fuel/air ratio by regulating the fuel flow to the main discharge nozzle. This is typically done by using a needle valve to vary the size of the main fuel metering passage or by adjusting the pressure in the float chamber.

question_text: An excessively rich mixture can be detected by :
option_a: black smoke from exhaust.
option_c: white smoke from exhaust.
option_d: a long purple flame from exhaust.
explanation: An excessively rich mixture means there is more fuel than can be completely burned by the available oxygen. This incomplete combustion produces carbon soot, which is visible as black smoke discharging from the exhaust pipe.

question_text: When leaning the mixture for the most economic cruise fuel flow, excessive leaning will cause :
option_a: high cylinder head and exhaust gas temperature
option_c: low cylinder head and exhaust gas temperature
option_d: high manifold pressure
explanation: If the fuel/air mixture is leaned excessively past the peak EGT point, the slower combustion rate can cause the fuel mixture to continue burning during the exhaust stroke. This results in dangerously high cylinder head temperatures (CHT) and exhaust gas temperatures (EGT).

question_text: The main purpose of the mixture control is to:
option_a: adjust the fuel flow to obtain the proper fuel/air ratio
option_b: decrease the air supplied to the engine
option_c: increase the oxygen supplied to the engine
option_d: decrease oxygen supplied to the engine
explanation: The primary purpose of the mixture control system is to allow the pilot to adjust the fuel flow to match the mass of air entering the engine. This maintains the correct fuel/air ratio across varying flight altitudes and ambient air densities.

question_text: Fuel/air ratio is the ratio between the:
option_a: mass of fuel and mass of air entering the cylinder.
option_b: volume of fuel and volume of air entering the carburettor.
option_c: volume of fuel and volume of air entering the cylinder.
option_d: mass of fuel and mass of air entering the carburettor
explanation: The fuel/air ratio is the ratio between the mass of fuel and the mass of air entering the engine cylinders. Using mass rather than volume is critical because air density changes significantly with altitude, while fuel density remains relatively constant.

question_text: Overheating of a piston engine is likely to result from an excessively :
option_a: weak mixture.
option_c: low barometric pressure.
option_d: high barometric pressure.
explanation: Operating a piston engine with an excessively weak (lean) mixture can cause overheating and high cylinder head temperatures. A lean mixture burns slower, which exposes the cylinder walls to high combustion temperatures for a longer duration of the stroke.

question_text: In a piston engine if the ratio of air to fuel, by weight, is approximately 9:1, the mixture is said to be :
option_a: rich
option_c: too weak to support combustion
option_d: normal
explanation: A stoichiometric mixture (ideal combustion) is approximately 15 parts of air to 1 part of fuel by weight. A ratio of 9:1 contains far more fuel than normal, making it a very rich mixture.

question_text: For a piston engine, the ideal fuel/air mixture corresponding to a richness of 1 is obtained for a weight ratio of:
explanation: The chemically correct fuel/air ratio for complete combustion (stoichiometric ratio) is 1 part of fuel to 15 parts of air by weight (or 1/15th). At this ratio, all oxygen and fuel are consumed during combustion.

question_text: (For this question use appendix )On the attached diagram showing the power output of a piston engine as a function of mixture richness, best economy is at the point marked:
explanation: On a diagram plotting engine power against mixture strength, the best economy setting is located at a mixture ratio that is slightly lean of stoichiometric (richness slightly less than 1), typically where fuel consumption per horsepower is minimized.

question_text: The richness of a fuel/air mixture ratio is the :
option_a: real mixture ratio relative to the theoretical ratio.
option_b: mass of fuel relative to the volume of air.
option_c: volume of fuel relative to the volume of air.
option_d: volume of fuel relative to the mass of the volume of air.
explanation: The richness of a fuel/air mixture is defined as the actual ratio of the mass of fuel to air, compared to the stoichiometric (theoretical) ratio required for complete combustion. A richness greater than 1 represents a rich mixture, while less than 1 is a lean mixture.

question_text: The feathering pump of a hydraulic variable-pitch propeller:
option_a: is an electrically driven oil pump, which supplies the propeller with pressure oil, when the engine is inoperative.
option_b: is intended to control the pitch setting of the propeller during flight in order to obtain a constant speed.
option_c: controls the propeller, if the speed governor fails.
option_d: is driven by the engine and supplies pressure oil to the propeller in case of engine problems.
explanation: The feathering pump is an independent, electrically driven oil pump that provides the high-pressure oil required to force the propeller blades into the feathered position. It operates independently of the engine, ensuring that pilots can feather the propeller even if the engine has failed and is inoperative.

question_text: Consider the variable-pitch propeller of a turbo-prop.During deceleration :
option_a: when braking, the propeller supplies negative thrust and absorbs engine power.
option_b: at zero power, the propeller thrust is zero and the engine power absorbed is nil.
option_c: when feathered, the propeller produces thrust and absorbs no engine power.
option_d: with propeller windmilling, the thrust is zero and the propeller supplies engine power.
explanation: When a turboprop decelerates on the ground, the propeller blades are moved into the beta (ground) range, providing negative blade angles. This causes the propeller to supply negative thrust (aerodynamic braking) while absorbing power from the engine.

question_text: The pitch angle of a constant-speed propeller
option_a: increases with increasing true air speed.
option_c: decreases with increasing true air speed.
option_d: is independent of the true air speed.
explanation: For a constant-speed propeller to maintain a constant RPM as the aircraft speeds up, the blade angle of attack must be kept at its optimum value. Consequently, the pitch angle of the blades will increase as the true airspeed (TAS) increases.

question_text: A propeller blade is twisted, so as to
option_a: keep the local Angle of Attack constant along the blade.
option_b: avoid the appearance of sonic phenomena.
option_c: decrease the blade tangential velocity from the blade root to the tip.
option_d: allow a higher mechanical stress.
explanation: A propeller blade is twisted from the root to the tip because the rotational velocity of the blade increases as you move outward from the hub. The twist gradually reduces the geometric pitch angle toward the tip, keeping the local aerodynamic angle of attack constant along the entire span of the blade.

question_text: A pilot normally uses the propeller autofeather system during :
option_a: Take-off and landing.
option_c: Take-off.
option_d: Landing.
explanation: The autofeather system automatically detects an engine failure and feathers the propeller to minimize drag. Because an engine failure at high power and low speed is most critical during takeoff, pilots normally arm and utilize this system during the takeoff phase.

question_text: When increasing true airspeed with a constant engine RPM, the angle of attack of a fixed pitch propeller :
option_a: reduces.
option_c: stays constant.
option_d: stays constant because it only varies with engine RPM.
explanation: In a fixed-pitch propeller, the blade angle is physically fixed. As the true airspeed (TAS) increases while RPM remains constant, the relative airflow meets the blade chord at a shallower angle, which reduces the blade's aerodynamic angle of attack.

question_text: When TAS increases, the pitch angle of a constant speed propeller (RPM and MAP levers are not moved) :
option_a: increases.
option_c: first reduces and after a short time increases to its previous value.
option_d: stays constant.
explanation: As true airspeed (TAS) increases, the relative wind meets the propeller blades at a shallower angle of attack, which reduces drag and tends to cause the engine to overspeed. The constant-speed governor senses this and increases the blade pitch angle to restore the selected RPM and maintain governor balance.

question_text: The main advantage of a constant speed propeller as compared to a fixed pitch propeller is a :
option_a: higher efficiency in all operating ranges.
option_b: constant efficiency in all operating ranges.
option_c: lower propeller blade stress.
option_d: higher efficiency in cruising range.
explanation: The primary advantage of a constant-speed propeller is its ability to automatically adjust its blade pitch to maintain the optimum angle of attack. This allows the propeller to operate at high aerodynamic efficiency across all flight phases, including takeoff, climb, and cruise.

question_text: To unfeather a propeller during flight you have to :
option_a: use the electric unfeathering pump.
option_c: gain speed for aerodynamic unfeathering.
option_d: gain speed so as to use the engine unfeathering pump.
explanation: To unfeather a propeller in flight, a dedicated electric unfeathering pump (or an accumulator containing trapped high-pressure oil) is activated. This high-pressure oil is directed to the propeller hub pitch change mechanism to force the blades out of the feathered position.

question_text: In case of engine failure during flight the blades of the constant speed propeller in a single engine aeroplane, not fitted with feathering system
option_a: move in the lowest pitch position by the centrifugal force.
option_b: move in low pitch position by oil pressure created by the windmilling propeller.
option_c: move in a certain pitch position depending on windmilling RPM.
option_d: move in the highest pitch position by the aerodynamical force.
explanation: In a single-engine aircraft not equipped with a feathering system, an engine failure removes the high-pressure engine oil holding the blades in high pitch. Consequently, centrifugal counterweights or spring forces will move the blades to the lowest pitch position to assist in engine windmilling.

question_text: For take-off, the correct combination of propeller pitch (1), and propeller lever position (2) at brake release is :
option_a: (1) low (2) forward.
option_c: (1) high (2) aft.
option_d: (1) high (2) forward.
