explanation: For takeoff, the pilot sets the propeller control lever fully forward to select the maximum RPM setting. This commands the governor to adjust the blades to a low pitch angle, which minimizes aerodynamic drag and allows the engine to develop maximum power at low airspeeds.

question_text: On a normally aspirated aero-engine fitted with a fixed pitch propeller :
option_a: manifold pressure decreases as the aircraft climbs at a fixed throttle setting.
option_b: the propeller setting is constant at all indicated airspeeds.
option_c: in level flight, manifold pressure will remain constant when the rpm is increased by opening the throttle.
option_d: in a descent at a fixed throttle setting manifold pressure will always remain constant.
explanation: On a normally aspirated engine, the manifold air pressure (MAP) decreases during a climb at a fixed throttle setting because the atmospheric pressure decreases with altitude. The engine's ability to draw in air decreases, leading to a natural drop in MAP.

question_text: An asymmetric loading (p-factor) on the propeller exists ..
option_a: If the aeroplane has a large angle of attack.
option_b: If there is an unbalanced propeller.
option_c: Only for counterrotating propeller
option_d: Only if the 'constant speed propeller' mechanism is broken.
explanation: Asymmetric propeller loading, or P-factor, occurs when the aircraft is operated at a high angle of attack. Because the propeller disc is tilted relative to the airflow, the descending blade has a higher relative velocity and angle of attack than the ascending blade, creating more thrust on one side.

question_text: In twin-engine aeroplanes with right turning propellers
option_a: the left engine is the critical motor.
option_b: the left engine produces a higher yaw moment if the right engine fails than vice versa.
option_c: the 'minimum control speed' is determined by the failure of the right engine.
option_d: the right engine is the critical motor.
explanation: In an aircraft with two conventional right-turning propellers, the thrust centerline of the right engine is further from the fuselage than the thrust centerline of the left engine. Consequently, failure of the left engine creates a much larger yawing moment, making the left engine the critical engine.

question_text: In general, in twin-engine aeroplanes with 'constant speed propeller'
option_a: the oil pressure turns the propeller blades towards smaller pitch angle.
option_b: the aerodynamic force turns the propeller blades towards higher pitch angle.
option_c: the spring force turns the propeller blades towards smaller pitch angle.
option_d: the oil pressure turns the propeller blades towards higher pitch angle.
explanation: In most multi-engine aircraft, the propeller is designed with safety counterweights and spring forces that naturally drive the blades toward high pitch to prevent drag during a failure. Therefore, the system utilizes high-pressure oil from the governor to force the blades toward a smaller (fine) pitch angle.

question_text: In modern aircraft, a pilot can actuate the feather system by :
option_a: pulling the RPM lever backwards.
option_c: pushing the power lever forward.
option_d: pulling the power levers backwards.
explanation: On modern aircraft, a pilot can manually feather a variable-pitch propeller by pulling the propeller (RPM) control lever fully backwards past the low RPM detent into the "feather" position. This action dumps the hydraulic oil from the propeller hub, allowing the springs and counterweights to feather the blades.

question_text: Fixed-pitch propellers are usually designed for maximum efficiency at :
option_a: cruising speed
option_c: full throttle
option_d: take-off
explanation: Fixed-pitch propellers are compromise designs since they cannot adjust their blade angles. They are usually designed to achieve maximum aerodynamic efficiency at the aircraft's normal cruising speed, where the aircraft spends the majority of its flight time.

question_text: Which of the following qualitative statements about a fixed propeller optimized for cruise condition, is true for the take-off case? The angle of attack of the propeller :
option_a: blade is relatively high.
option_c: airfoil section is negative.
option_d: blades reduces to zero.
explanation: A fixed-pitch propeller optimized for cruise has a relatively large blade pitch angle to match high cruise speeds. During takeoff, when the aircraft's forward speed is low, the relative wind meets this coarse blade at a very high angle of attack, which can cause the blades to stall.

question_text: The 'constant speed propeller' has
option_a: only above and below the design point a better efficiency than the fixed propeller with the same design speed.
option_b: in general a worse efficiency than the fixed propeller.
option_c: only at the design speed a better efficiency than the fixed propeller.
option_d: its best efficiency during climb.
explanation: Unlike a fixed-pitch propeller, which only operates at peak efficiency at its single design speed, a constant-speed propeller maintains high efficiency across a wide range of speeds. This gives it a significantly better efficiency than a fixed propeller above and below the fixed propeller's design point.

question_text: What will happen to the geometrical pitch angle of a ""constant speed propeller"" if the manifold pressure is increased ?
option_a: It will increase
option_b: It will increase and after a short time it will be the same again
option_c: It will decrease so that the engine can increase
option_d: It will remain the same
explanation: When manifold pressure is increased, the engine produces more torque, which tends to accelerate the propeller and increase RPM. The governor detects this speed increase and automatically increases the geometrical pitch angle of the blades to increase drag and maintain the selected RPM.

question_text: The 'slipstream effect' of a propeller is most prominent at:
option_a: low airspeeds with high power setting.
option_b: high airspeeds with low power setting.
option_c: high airspeeds with high power setting.
option_d: low airspeeds with low power setting.
explanation: The slipstream effect (the spiraling air column from the propeller hitting the vertical stabilizer) is most pronounced when the propeller is generating maximum thrust and the air speed is low. This corresponds to flight at low airspeeds with high power settings, such as during takeoff.

question_text: The pitch angle of a propeller is the angle between the :
option_a: reference chord line and the propeller plane of rotation.
option_b: propeller reference chord line and the relative airflow.
option_c: propeller reference chord line and the extremity of the propeller.
option_d: propeller plane of rotation and the relative airflow.
explanation: The pitch (or blade) angle of a propeller is defined as the angle between the reference chord line of the propeller blade section and the plane of rotation of the propeller disc.

question_text: When in flight, a piston engine is stopped and the propeller blade pitch angle is near 90°, the propeller is said to be...
option_a: feathered.
option_c: transparent.
option_d: at zero drag.
explanation: When an engine fails in flight, the propeller blades are rotated so that their chord lines are aligned parallel to the relative wind (a blade angle of approximately 90 degrees). In this state, the propeller is said to be feathered, which stops it from rotating and minimizes aerodynamic drag.

question_text: During a power change on an engine equipped with a constant speed propeller, a wrong combination of manifold pressure and RPM values results in excessive pressures in the cylinders. This is the case when one simultaneously selects a ...
option_a: high manifold pressure and low RPM.
option_b: low manifold pressure and high RPM.
option_c: high manifold pressure and high RPM.
option_d: low manifold pressure and low RPM.
explanation: Selecting a high manifold pressure (high engine loading) in combination with a low RPM (slow piston movement) creates high cylinder pressures and can lead to detonation. This condition, often called "running oversquare," places severe mechanical stresses on the cylinders and pistons.

question_text: From the cruise, with all the parameters correctly set, if the altitude is reduced, to maintain the same mixture the fuel flow should:
option_a: increase
option_c: remain the same
option_d: increase or decrease, depending on the engine type
explanation: As altitude is reduced, the ambient air density increases, meaning there is more oxygen by weight entering the cylinders. To maintain the same fuel/air mixture ratio and prevent the engine from running too lean, the fuel flow must be increased.

question_text: When applying carburettor heating :
option_a: the mixture becomes richer.
option_b: a decrease in RPM results from the lean mixture.
option_c: the mixture becomes leaner.
option_d: no change occurs in the mixture ratio.
explanation: Applying carburettor heat introduces warm, less-dense air into the engine intake. Since the mass of the entering air decreases while the fuel flow remains constant, the fuel/air mixture becomes richer.

question_text: When the pilot moves the mixture lever of a piston engine towards a lean position the :
option_a: amount of fuel entering the combustion chamber is reduced.
option_b: volume of air entering the carburettor is reduced.
option_c: amount of fuel entering the combustion chamber is increased.
option_d: volume of air entering the carburettor is increased.
explanation: When the pilot moves the mixture control lever toward the lean position, the fuel metering valve inside the carburettor or fuel control unit is adjusted to restrict fuel flow. This reduces the amount of fuel entering the combustion chambers relative to the airflow.

question_text: When altitude increases without adjustment of the mixture ratio, the piston engine performance is affected because of a :
option_a: decrease of air density for a constant quantity of fuel.
option_b: constant air density for a bigger quantity of fuel.
option_c: increase of air density for smaller quantity of fuel.
option_d: decrease of air density for a smaller quantity of fuel.
explanation: As an aircraft climbs, the density of the atmospheric air decreases, reducing the mass of oxygen entering the induction system. If the fuel flow is not adjusted (restricting fuel flow), the mixture will become progressively richer, degrading engine performance.

question_text: When changing power on engines equipped with constant-speed propeller, engine overload is avoided by :
option_a: increasing the RPM before increasing the manifold pressure.
option_b: adjusting Fuel Flow before the manifold pressure.
option_c: reducing the RPM before reducing the manifold pressure.
option_d: increasing the manifold pressure before increasing the RPM.
explanation: To avoid overstressing the cylinders when changing power settings on a constant-speed propeller system, the pilot must follow a specific sequence. When increasing power, the RPM must be increased before the manifold pressure; when decreasing power, manifold pressure is reduced before RPM.

question_text: To adjust the mixture ratio of a piston engine when altitude increases, means to:
option_a: decrease the fuel flow in order to compensate for the decreasing air density.
option_b: decrease the amount of fuel in the mixture in order to compensate for the increasing air density.
option_c: increase the amount of fuel in the mixture to compensate for the decreasing air pressure and density.
option_d: increase the mixture ratio.
explanation: Adjusting the mixture ratio as altitude increases means leaning the mixture. This is accomplished by decreasing the fuel flow to compensate for the reduced density of the air at higher altitudes, maintaining the optimum fuel/air ratio.

question_text: The maximum horsepower output which can be obtained from an engine when it is operated at specified rpm and manifold pressure conditons established as safe for continuous operation is termed :
option_a: rated power.
option_c: take-off power.
option_d: critical power.
explanation: Rated power (or maximum continuous power) is the maximum horsepower output that an engine can safely produce continuously under specified RPM and manifold pressure conditions, without causing damage or overheating.

question_text: With which instrument(s) do you monitor the power output of an aeroplane fitted with a fixed pitch propeller?
option_a: RPM indicator.
option_c: RPM and MAP indicator.
option_d: RPM and EGT indicator.
explanation: On an aircraft equipped with a fixed-pitch propeller, the propeller rotational speed is directly linked to the engine power output. Therefore, the tachometer (RPM indicator) is the primary instrument used by the pilot to monitor engine power.

question_text: An EGT (Exhaust Gas Temperature) indicator for a piston engine is used to :
option_a: assist the pilot to settle correct mixture.
option_c: control the carburator inlet air flow.
option_d: control the fuel temperature.
explanation: The Exhaust Gas Temperature (EGT) indicator measures the temperature of the exhaust gases leaving the cylinders. It is used by the pilot as a precise guide to adjust the fuel flow (using the mixture control) to achieve the best economy or best power setting.

question_text: During climb with constant throttle and RPM lever setting (mixture being constant) the :
option_a: Manifold Air Pressure (MAP) decreases.
option_c: Manifold Air Pressure (MAP) increases.
option_d: RPM increases.
explanation: During a climb with constant throttle and RPM settings in a normally aspirated engine, the ambient atmospheric pressure drops. Consequently, the Manifold Air Pressure (MAP) will decrease as the aircraft gains altitude.

question_text: The conditions which can cause knocking are :
option_a: High manifold pressure and low revolutions per minute.
option_b: High manifold pressure and high revolutions per minute.
option_c: Low manifold pressure and high revolutions per minute.
option_d: Low manifold pressure and high fuel flow.
explanation: Knocking (or detonation) is caused by excessive pressure and temperature in the cylinders, which leads to the fuel/air mixture exploding rather than burning smoothly. This is most likely to occur under high manifold pressure and low RPM settings.

question_text: Which of the following factors would be likely to increase the possibility of detonation occurring within a piston engine ?
option_a: using too lean a fuel/air mixture ratio
option_b: the use of a fuel with a high octane rating as compared to the use of one with a low octane rating
option_c: using an engine with a low compression ratio
option_d: slightly retarding the ignition timing
explanation: Detonation is the uncontrolled, explosive ignition of the fuel/air mixture in the cylinder. It is highly promoted by operating the engine with an excessively lean mixture, which raises cylinder head temperatures and combustion speeds.

question_text: On a a normally aspirated engine (non turbo-charged), the manifold pressure gauge always indicates...
option_a: a lower value than atmospheric pressure when the engine is running.
option_b: a greater value than atmospheric pressure when the engine is running.
option_c: zero on the ground when the engine is stopped.
option_d: a value equal to the QFE when the engine is at full power on the ground.
explanation: On a normally aspirated engine, the intake system relies on piston suction to draw in air, which creates a vacuum. Therefore, when the engine is running, the manifold pressure gauge will always indicate a lower pressure than the ambient atmospheric pressure.

question_text: Spark plug fouling is more likely to happen if :
option_a: the aircraft climbs without mixture adjustment.
option_b: the aircraft descends without a mixture adjustment.
option_c: power is increased too abruptly.
option_d: the engine runs at the authorized maximum continuous power for too long.
explanation: Spark plug fouling occurs when carbon or lead deposits accumulate on the plug electrodes, which is caused by incomplete combustion. This is most likely to happen when the aircraft climbs without leaning the mixture, resulting in an excessively rich fuel mixture.

question_text: Pre-ignition refers to the condition that may arise when :
option_a: the mixture is ignited by abnormal conditions within the cylinder before the spark occurs at the plug
option_b: the mixture is ignited before the piston has reached top dead centre.
option_c: a rich mixture is ignited by the sparking plugs.
option_d: the sparking plug ignites the mixture too early.
explanation: Pre-ignition is the premature ignition of the fuel/air mixture before the spark plug fires, caused by local hot spots in the cylinder (such as glowing carbon deposits or overheated spark plug electrodes). It occurs independently of the normal spark timing.

question_text: With a piston engine, when detonation is recognised, you:
option_a: Reduce manifold pressure and enrich the mixture
option_b: Reduce manifold pressure and lean the mixture
option_c: Increase manifold pressure and enrich the mixture
option_d: Increase manifold pressure and lean the mixture
explanation: If detonation is recognized (indicated by engine knocking or a rapid rise in CHT), the pilot must immediately reduce the thermal and mechanical stresses on the cylinders. This is accomplished by reducing the manifold pressure (reducing throttle) and enriching the mixture to provide cooling.

question_text: In a turbo-jet, the purpose of the turbine is to ...
option_a: drive the compressor by using part of the energy from the exhaust gases
option_b: clear the burnt gases, the expansion of which provide the thrust
option_c: compress the air in order to provide a better charge of the combustion chamber
option_d: drive devices like pumps, regulator, generator.
explanation: The primary purpose of the turbine in a turbojet engine is to extract mechanical energy from the high-temperature, high-velocity exhaust gases. This extracted energy is transmitted through a central shaft to drive the compressor and engine accessories.

question_text: (Use the appendix to answer this question)The gas turbine illustrated is of the following type:
option_a: free turbine and centrifugal compressor
option_c: single shaft turbine and centrifugal compressor
option_d: single shaft turbine and axial compressor
explanation: A free-turbine engine with a centrifugal compressor is typical for turboshaft/turboprop designs where the gas generator section is mechanically independent of the power turbine that drives the output shaft.

question_text: The purpose of the blow-in-doors at the air inlets is to:
option_a: provide the engine with additional air at high power settings and low air speeds.
option_b: provide the engine with additional air at high power settings at cruising speed.
option_c: feed cooling air to the engine cowling.
option_d: serve to increase the relative velocity at the first compressor stage.
explanation: Blow-in doors are auxiliary air inlets located in the engine cowl. They open automatically under high engine power settings at low airspeeds (such as during takeoff) to provide the engine compressor with the necessary additional mass flow of air.

question_text: In a compressor stage of a jet engine, the sequence is:
option_a: rotor - stator
option_c: rotor - rotor - stator
option_d: stator - stator - rotor
explanation: A single stage of an axial flow compressor consists of a rotating row of blades followed by a stationary row of blades. Therefore, the correct mechanical sequence in a compressor stage is rotor followed by stator.

question_text: In a single spool gas turbine engine, the compressor rpm is :
option_a: the same as turbine rpm.
option_c: greater than turbine rpm.
option_d: less than turbine rpm.
explanation: In a single-spool gas turbine engine, the compressor and the turbine are mounted on the same physical shaft. Consequently, the compressor rotational speed (RPM) is always exactly the same as the turbine RPM.

question_text: In the axial flow compressor of a turbo-jet engine, the flow duct is tapered. Its shape is calculated so as to:
option_a: maintain a constant axial speed in cruising flight.
option_b: maintain a constant axial speed whatever the engine rating.
option_c: reduce the axial speed in cruising flight.
option_d: reduce the axial speed, whatever the engine rating.
explanation: The flow duct of an axial compressor is tapered (decreasing in cross-sectional area from front to back). This shape is designed to maintain a constant axial velocity of the air as its pressure and density increase through successive compressor stages.

question_text: The compressor surge effect during acceleration is prevented by the :
option_a: Fuel Control Unit (F.C.U.).
option_c: surge bleed valves.
option_d: variable setting type nozzle guide vanes.
explanation: Compressor surge is a complete breakdown of airflow through the compressor. During rapid engine accelerations, surge is prevented by using automatic surge bleed valves that dump excess air from intermediate compressor stages to maintain stable airflow.

question_text: Concerning the centrifugal compressor, the compressor diffuser is a device in which the:
option_a: pressure rises and velocity falls.
option_b: pressure rises at a constant velocity.
option_c: velocity, pressure and temperature rise.
option_d: velocity rises and pressure falls.
explanation: The diffuser in a centrifugal compressor is a divergent passage located downstream of the impeller. As the high-velocity air passes through the diffuser, its velocity falls, which converts the kinetic energy into static pressure, causing the pressure to rise.

question_text: The fan in a high by-pass ratio turbo-jet engine produces:
option_a: the greater part of the thrust.
option_c: the lesser part of the thrust.
option_d: none of the thrust.
explanation: In a high-bypass ratio turbofan engine, the large diameter fan accelerates a massive volume of cold bypass air. This bypass airflow generates the vast majority (typically 75% to 80%) of the engine's total thrust.

question_text: In a gas turbine engine, compressor blades, which are not rigidly fixed in position when the engine is stationary, take up a rigid position when the engine is running due to :
option_a: the resultant of aerodynamic and centrifugal forces.
option_c: thermal expansion.
option_d: blade creep.
explanation: On many gas turbine engines, the compressor blades are pinned loosely in the rotor disc when stationary to allow for thermal expansion and damp vibrations. Once the engine runs, centrifugal force combined with aerodynamic lift forces locks the blades rigidly in their correct radial operating positions.

question_text: The primary purpose of the bleed valves fitted to axial flow compressors is to :
option_a: reduce the likelihood of compressor stall.
option_b: control the acceleration time of the engine.
option_c: spill compressor air should the engine overspeed thus controlling the speed.
option_d: enable an external air supply to spin up the compressor for engine starting.
explanation: The primary purpose of compressor bleed valves is to protect the engine from compressor stall or surge, especially during starting and acceleration. They automatically open at low RPM to vent excess air from intermediate stages, maintaining stable airflow velocities through the compressor.

question_text: The disadvantages of axial flow compressors compared to centrifugal flow compressors are :1 - expensive to manufacture2 - limited airflow3 - greater vulnerability to foreign object damage4 - limited compression ratioThe combination of correct answers is :
option_a: 03-Jan
option_c: 03-Fev
option_d: 04-Fev
explanation: Axial flow compressors are highly complex, consisting of thousands of individual blades, making them expensive to manufacture. Additionally, their open frontal design and thin, precise blades make them far more vulnerable to foreign object damage (FOD) compared to robust centrifugal compressors.

question_text: A stage in an axial compressor:
option_a: is made of a rotor disc followed by a row of stator blades
option_b: has a compression ratio in the order of 2.1
option_c: is made of row of stator blades followed by a rotor disc
option_d: has a compression ration in the order of 0.8
explanation: An individual stage of an axial flow compressor consists of a rotating row of blades (the rotor disc) followed by a stationary row of blades (the stator). The rotor accelerates the air, and the stator converts this kinetic energy into static pressure.

question_text: In a gas turbine engine, the maximum gas temperature is attained:
option_a: within the combustion chamber.
option_c: in the cooling airflow around the flame tube.
option_d: at the entry to the exhaust unit.
explanation: Within a gas turbine engine, the highest gas temperature is reached within the combustion chamber, specifically inside the primary combustion zone where fuel is burned with air. The temperature is then reduced by cooling air before entering the turbine.

question_text: When the combustion gases pass through a turbine the :
option_a: pressure drops.
option_c: velocity decreases.
option_d: temperature increases.
explanation: As high-pressure, high-temperature combustion gases pass through the turbine rotor blades, they expand and perform mechanical work. This expansion causes the gas pressure and temperature to drop as energy is extracted.

question_text: In the stator of a turbine, the speed V and static pressure Ps vary as follows:
option_a: V increases, Ps decreases.
option_c: V increases, Ps increases.
option_d: V decreases, Ps decreases.
explanation: The stator (nozzle guide vanes) of a turbine stage forms a series of convergent nozzles. As gases flow through these convergent passages, the velocity increases due to the nozzle effect, and the static pressure decreases.

question_text: An impulse turbine is a turbine in which the expansion takes place:
option_a: fully in the stator.
option_c: in the stator and in the rotor.
option_d: in order to produce a degree of jet propulsion < 1/2.
explanation: In a pure impulse turbine stage, the entire pressure drop of the gas occurs across the stationary nozzle guide vanes (stator). The gas velocity increases in the stator, and the rotor blades simply convert this kinetic energy into mechanical torque without any further pressure drop.

question_text: A ""fan"" stage of a ducted-fan turbine engine is driven by:
option_a: the low pressure turbine.
option_b: the high pressure compressor through reduction gearing.
option_c: the high pressure turbine.
option_d: airflow drawn across it by the high pressure compressor.
explanation: In a turbofan engine, the forward fan stage is driven by the low-pressure turbine (LPT). The LPT is located at the rear of the turbine section and is connected to the fan via an inner concentric shaft running through the center of the engine.

question_text: In a free turbine engine:
option_a: there is no mechanical connection between the compressor and the power output shaft.
option_b: its shaft may be connected to either a compressor or another turbine.
option_c: the air enters the compressor via the input turbine.
option_d: the compressor and power output shaft are mechanically connected.
explanation: In a free-turbine engine, the gas generator section is mechanically independent of the power turbine. The power turbine is driven solely by the gas flow and drives the propeller or output shaft without a mechanical connection to the compressor spool.

question_text: The primary reason for a limitation being imposed on the temperature of gas flow is to :
option_a: ensure that the maximum acceptable temperature at the turbine blades is not exceeded.
option_b: prevent damage to the jet pipe from overheating.
option_c: prevent overheating and subsequent creep of the nozzle guide vanes.
option_d: ensure that the maximum acceptable temperature within the combustion chamber is not exceeded.
explanation: The primary limit on gas temperature in a gas turbine engine is to protect the turbine rotor blades from structural failure. Excessive heat causes the metallic blades to weaken and experience "creep" (gradual stretching) under the intense centrifugal forces of rotation.

question_text: Turbine blade stages may be classed as either ""impulse"" or ""reaction"". In an impulse blade section :
option_a: the pressure drops across the nozzle guide vanes and remains constant across the rotor blades .
option_b: the pressure rises across the nozzle guide vanes and remains constant across the rotor blades .
option_c: the pressure remains constant across the nozzle guide vanes and drops across the rotor blades .
option_d: the pressure remains constant across the nozzle guide vanes and rises constant across the rotor blades .
explanation: In an impulse turbine stage, the pressure drops across the stationary nozzle guide vanes (stator) to accelerate the gas flow, but remains constant across the rotating rotor blades. The rotor blades only change the direction of the gas flow to extract energy.

question_text: For a fan jet engine, the by-pass ratio is the:
option_a: external airflow mass divided by the internal airflow mass
option_b: internal airflow mass divided by the external airflow mass
option_c: internal airflow mass divided by the fuelflow mass
option_d: fuelflow mass divided by the internal airflow mass
explanation: For a turbofan engine, the bypass ratio is defined as the ratio of the mass flow rate of air that passes through the fan duct (bypassing the engine core) to the mass flow rate of air that enters the engine core.

question_text: A reverse thrust door warning light on the flight deck instrument panel illuminates when:
option_a: the reverser doors are unlocked.
option_c: reverse has been selected but the doors have remained locked.
option_d: the reverser doors have moved to the reverse thrust position.
explanation: The reverse thrust door warning light on the flight deck instrument panel illuminates to warn the flight crew whenever the thrust reverser doors or translation sleeves are unlocked or not in their fully stowed position.

question_text: At constant fuel flow, if engine compressor air is bled off for engine anti-icing or a similar system, the turbine temperature:
option_a: will rise.
option_c: may rise or fall depending on which stage of the compressor is used for the bleed and the rpm of the engine at the moment of selection.
option_d: will fall.
explanation: If compressor bleed air is switched on while the fuel flow remains constant, the mass flow of air entering the combustion chamber is reduced. With less air to absorb the heat of combustion, the fuel/air ratio increases, causing the turbine gas temperature to rise.

question_text: If air is tapped from a gas turbine HP compressor, the effect on the engine pressure ratio (EPR) and the exhaust gas temperature (EGT) is that :
option_a: EPR decreases and EGT increases.
option_c: EPR decreases and EGT remains constant.
option_d: EPR remains constant and EGT increases.
explanation: Bleeding air from the high-pressure compressor reduces the pressure at the turbine inlet, which decreases the Engine Pressure Ratio (EPR). Additionally, because less air is available to cool the combustion chamber, the Exhaust Gas Temperature (EGT) increases.

question_text: Using compressor bleed air to power systems:
option_a: decreases aircraft performance
option_b: has no influence on aircraft performance
option_c: increases aircraft performance
option_d: is limited to the phases of take-off and landing
explanation: Tapping high-pressure bleed air from the compressor drains energetic air that would otherwise produce thrust. Consequently, using bleed air to power systems (like air conditioning or anti-ice) decreases overall engine thrust and aircraft performance.

question_text: The accessory units driven by the accessory gearbox of a turbo-jet engine are the :1. tacho-generator N12. tacho-generator N23. thrust reverser pneumatic motors4. AC generator and its Constant Speed Unit (CSD)5. oil pumps6. hydraulic pumps7. high pressure fuel pumpsThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is :
explanation: The accessory gearbox is driven by the high-pressure rotor spool via a radial drive shaft. It drives essential engine and aircraft accessories, including the N1 tacho-generator, the AC generator and its CSD, oil pumps, hydraulic pumps, and high-pressure fuel pumps.

question_text: The use of igniters is necessary on a turbo-jet:1 - throughout the operating range of the engine2 - for accelerations3 - for ground starts4 - for in-flight relights5 - during turbulence in flight6 - under heavy precipitation or in icing conditionsThe combination which regroups all of the correct statements is :
explanation: Igniters in a jet engine are not run continuously during normal flight. They are activated for ground starting, in-flight engine relights, and as a precaution during flight through heavy precipitation, icing conditions, or severe turbulence to prevent flameout.

question_text: For a turbine engine, the term self-sustaining speed relates to the speed at which the engine :
option_a: will run without any external assistance.
option_b: is designed to idle after starting.
option_c: operates most efficiently in the cruise..
option_d: will enable the generators to supply bus-bar voltage.
explanation: Self-sustaining speed is the minimum engine rotational speed (RPM) at which the turbine extracts sufficient energy from the gas flow to drive the compressor and engine accessories without any assistance from the starter motor.

question_text: An impulse coupling does not function at such speeds above those encountered in starting. Its engaging pawls are prevented from operating at higher speeds by
option_a: centrifugal force
option_c: a coil spring
option_d: electro-magnetic action of operating magneto.
explanation: The impulse coupling is only designed to function at low starting speeds. Once the engine starts and accelerates, centrifugal force acts on the pivoting pawls inside the coupling, pulling them outward and disengaging them to prevent operation at higher speeds.

question_text: A ""hung start"" is the failure of an engine to accelerate to its normal idle speed. It may be caused by:
option_a: an attempt to ignite the fuel before the engine has been accelerated sufficiently by the starter.
option_c: the starter cutting out early in the starting sequence before the engine has accelerated to the required rpm for ignition.
option_d: failure of the fuel to ignite in the starting sequence after the engine has been accelerated to the required rpm by the starter.
explanation: A hung start occurs when the engine ignites but fails to accelerate to its normal idle RPM, remaining stabilized at a low speed. This is typically caused by insufficient starter power, early starter cutout, or a fuel scheduling problem.

question_text: The pressure usually produced by the Boost Pumps (BP) of the fuel supply system is within the following range:
option_a: 20 to 50 psi
option_d: 300 to 500 psi
explanation: The low-pressure fuel boost pumps located inside the fuel tanks supply fuel to the engine-driven high-pressure pumps. They typically operate in a low-pressure range of 20 to 50 psi to prevent fuel vaporization in the lines.

question_text: The purpose of the barometric correction in a fuel controller is to:
option_a: maintain the correct weight fuel to air ratio when the altitude increases.
option_b: reduce the fuel-to-air ratio when altitude increases.
option_c: increase the fuel-to-air ratio when altitude increases.
option_d: maintain a constant fuel metering whatever the altitude.
explanation: As altitude increases, the ambient air density decreases, meaning there is less oxygen by weight entering the engine. The barometric correction unit in the fuel control system automatically reduces the fuel flow to maintain the correct fuel-to-air ratio.

question_text: (For this question use annex 021-4008A)Reference should be made to the fuel sypply system shown in annex.In flight, with center tank empty and APU operating, a fuel unbalance is detected (quantity in tank 1 < quantity in tank 2).Rebalancing of the two tanks is:
option_a: possible with ""CROSSFEED"" open and tank 1 pumps ""OFF"" and tank 2 pumps ""ON"".
option_b: impossible without causing the APU stop.
option_c: possible with ""CROSSFEED"" open and tank 2 pumps ""OFF"".
option_d: impossible because there is no fuel in center tank.
explanation: To correct a fuel imbalance where Tank 1 has less fuel than Tank 2, the crossfeed valve must be opened, the fuel pumps in Tank 1 switched OFF, and the pumps in Tank 2 left ON, feeding both engines from Tank 2.

question_text: In a gas turbine engine, the power changes are normally made by controlling the amount of:
option_a: fuel supplied.
option_c: air leaving the compressor by the opening or closing of bleed valves.
option_d: air entering the compressor and fuel entering the combustion chambers.
explanation: In a gas turbine engine, thrust is controlled by adjusting the rate of fuel flow injected into the combustion chamber. Increasing fuel flow raises the gas temperature, which increases turbine speed and airflow, thereby increasing thrust.

question_text: In a fuel system, the oil to fuel heat exchanger allows:
option_a: jet engine oil cooling through thermal exchange with fuel flowing from tanks.
option_b: fuel cooling so as to prevent vapour creation likely to unprime nozzles.
option_c: fuel heating as required whenever fuel filter clogging is detected.
option_d: automatic fuel heating by the engine oil so as to prevent icing in fuel filter.
explanation: The oil-to-fuel heat exchanger acts as a cooler for the hot engine lubricating oil and a heater for the cold fuel. Heating the fuel is highly beneficial as it prevents ice crystals from forming and clogging the low-pressure fuel filter in cold weather.

question_text: The reason for having a low pressure fuel-cooled oil cooler in a recirculatory type oil system is to:
option_a: cool the oil and heat the fuel.
option_c: cool both the oil and the fuel.
option_d: heat the fuel only.
explanation: The fuel-cooled oil cooler is a heat exchanger that cools the hot engine oil returning to the tank while simultaneously heating the fuel flowing to the engine. This thermal exchange serves both purposes, improving fuel efficiency and maintaining safe oil temperatures.

question_text: In very cold weather, the pilot notices during startup, a slightly higher than normal oil pressure.This higher pressure :
option_a: is normal, if it decreases after startup.
option_b: is abnormal and requires the engine to be shut down.
option_c: is abnormal but does not require the engine to be shut down.
option_d: requires an oil change.
explanation: In very cold weather, the engine lubricating oil is highly viscous, which causes a higher flow resistance and elevated pressure on startup. This is normal, provided the oil pressure returns to its normal operating range as the engine warms up.

question_text: The fuel temperature, at which, under standard conditions, the vapour ignites in contact with a flame and extinguishs immediately, is the:
option_a: flash point
option_c: fire point
option_d: self ignition point
explanation: The flash point of a liquid fuel is the lowest temperature at which it releases enough vapor to form an ignitable mixture with air. At this temperature, the vapor will momentarily ignite in contact with a flame but will not sustain combustion.

question_text: An engine pressure ratio (EPR) gauge reading normally shows the ratio of:
option_a: jet pipe pressure to compressor inlet pressure.
option_b: jet pipe pressure to combustion chamber pressure.
option_c: combustion chamber pressure to compressor inlet pressure.
option_d: compressor outlet pressure to compressor inlet pressure.
explanation: The Engine Pressure Ratio (EPR) gauge measures the ratio of the total pressure at the turbine discharge to the total pressure at the compressor inlet. It is used as a primary indication of thrust on many engines.

question_text: The thrust of a turbo-jet, at the selection of full power :1 - equals the product of the exhaust gas mass flow and the exhaust gas velocity2 - is obtained by pressure of the exhaust gas on the ambient air3 - is equivalent to zero mechanical power since the aeroplane is not moving4 - is independant of the outside air temperatureThe combination which regroups all of the correct statements is :
option_a: 03-Jan
option_c: 03-Fev
explanation: The thrust generated by a turbojet engine is primarily the product of the exhaust gas mass flow rate and the exhaust velocity. Additionally, if the aircraft is stationary on the ground, the mechanical power output is technically zero since no distance is being covered.

question_text: Consider a jet engine whose control is based on the Engine Pressure Ratio (EPR):1. with a constant EPR, the thrust decreases when the altitude increases2. with a constant EPR, the thrust is independent of the Mach number3. At same environmental conditions, a given EPR setting maintains the thrust irrespective of engine wear due to ageing.4. the EPR is determined by the impact pressure difference between the turbine outlet and the compressor inlet5. on take-off, in the event of icing not detected by the crew, the indicated EPR is lower than the real EPRThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is :
explanation: At a constant EPR, the density of the air decreases with altitude, which causes a reduction in the mass flow rate and a decrease in thrust. Additionally, a given EPR setting will maintain a consistent thrust target under the same environmental conditions, compensating for normal engine wear.

question_text: The Engine Pressure Ratio (EPR) is the ratio of:
option_a: the total turbine outlet pressure to the total compressor inlet pressure.
option_b: the total turbine outlet pressure to the total compressor outlet pressure.
option_c: the total turbine inlet pressure to the total compressor inlet pressure.
option_d: the total turbine inlet pressure to the total compressor outlet pressure.
explanation: Engine Pressure Ratio (EPR) is defined as the ratio of the total turbine outlet pressure to the total compressor inlet pressure. It is used to monitor and set thrust on engines where pressure ratio correlates directly with thrust output.

question_text: The control of free turbine engines on turboprops, is accomplished by:- a propeller control lever used to select: 1 - propeller RPM 2 - turbine temperature 3 - turbine RPM- a fuel control lever used to select: 4 - propeller RPM 5 - torque 6 - turbine temperature The combination which regroups all of the correct statements is :
explanation: On a turboprop with a free turbine, the propeller control lever is used to select the desired propeller RPM (adjusting the governor). The power lever is used to regulate the torque by adjusting the fuel flow to the gas generator.

question_text: On the ground, the Auxiliary Power Unit (APU) can be substituted for the:
option_a: ground power unit, the starting system, the air conditioning unit.
option_b: ground power unit, the air conditioning unit.
option_c: ground power unit, the starting system.
option_d: ground power unit.
explanation: When an aircraft is parked on the ground with engines shut down, the Auxiliary Power Unit (APU) can supply electrical power, high-pressure bleed air for engine starting, and pneumatic pressure for the air conditioning system, substituting for ground carts.

question_text: A modern Auxiliary Power Unit (APU) is designed to provide power for ground starting of an engine. It also supplies both in the air (subject to certification limitations) and on the ground :
option_a: air conditioning and electrical services.
option_b: air conditioning and thrust in the event of engine failure.
option_c: either air conditioning or electrical services, but never both at the same time.
option_d: air conditioning and electrical services (on the ground) electrical and hydraulic back-up services (in the air).
explanation: In addition to ground engine starting, the APU is designed to operate both on the ground and in flight (up to specific altitude limits) to supply the aircraft with three-phase electrical power and pneumatic air for air conditioning.

question_text: In addition to fire detention/protection, most auxiliary power units (APUs) have automatic controls for stating, stopping and maintaining operation within safe limits. These controls provide correct sequencing of the starting cycle as well as protection against :
option_a: high turbine gas temperature (TGT), overspeed, loss of oil pressure and high oil temperature.
option_b: high TGT and loss of oil pressure only.
option_c: overspeed and high oil temperature only.
option_d: high TGT only.
explanation: The APU control system monitors critical operating parameters to protect the unit. It will automatically shut down the APU if it detects an overspeed condition, high turbine gas temperature (TGT), low oil pressure, or high oil temperature.

question_text: Some emergency exits must be equipped with devices so as to help the occupants to get out and reach the ground if their threshold is at a height above the ground greater than:
option_a: 6 ft, aeroplane on the ground, landing gear extended.
option_b: 6 ft, aeroplane on the ground, one main gear or nose gear collapse.
option_c: 8 ft, aeroplane on the ground, one main gear or nose gear collapse.
option_d: 8 ft, aeroplane on the ground, landing gear extended.
explanation: Under airworthiness regulations, emergency exits must be equipped with an assisted evacuation device (such as an escape slide) if the threshold height of the exit is more than 6 feet above the ground with the landing gear extended.

question_text: The number of emergency exits in transport aeroplanes
option_a: must be arranged to allow all passengers and all crew members to leave the aeroplane within 90 sec. through 50 % of the available emergency exits.
option_b: must be arranged to allow at least 50 % of all passengers to leave the aeroplane within 2 minutes.
option_c: depends on the decision of the manufacturer in agreement with the operator.
option_d: must be in accordance with the number of passengers on board.
explanation: Aircraft emergency exits must be sized and arranged to allow a full evacuation of all passengers and crew within 90 seconds. This demonstration must show that the evacuation can be completed even with 50% of the available emergency exits blocked.

question_text: A manual inflation handle:
option_a: serves to actuate inflation of a slide when automatic inflation fails
option_b: serves to inflate a life jacket when the normal inflation function fails
option_c: operates a hand pump for manual inflation of a slide
option_d: is generally not applied on slides.
explanation: Emergency escape slides are designed to inflate automatically when the door is opened in the armed mode. If the automatic inflation system fails to trigger, the cabin crew must pull the manual inflation handle to actuate the gas cylinder and inflate the slide.

question_text: The purpose of the proximity of the emergency evacuation path marking system is to :
option_a: replace the overhead emergency lighting during an emergency evacuation with a thick smoke.
option_b: replace the overhead emergency lighting in case of failure.
option_c: mark only the exits at the floor level.
option_d: to be used only at night.
explanation: The floor-proximity emergency path marking system consists of lights or photoluminescent strips along the cabin aisle. Its purpose is to guide passengers to emergency exits in conditions where the overhead emergency lights are obscured by dense smoke.

question_text: An exit is considered to be out of service when the following elements are inoperative the:1. external door opening mechanism2. internal door opening mechanism3. door opening aid device4. open door locking system5. auxiliary means of evacuation6. emergency lightingThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: An emergency exit is considered completely out of service if any of its critical components are inoperative. This includes the inner and outer opening mechanisms, the opening aid, the door hold-open lock, the escape slide, or the exit emergency lighting.

question_text: Evacuation slide inflation is ensured by :
option_a: a pressurized gas canister combined with the slide itself.
option_c: a manual pump, used when needed by the cabin crew.
option_d: pressurized air from the air conditioning system.
explanation: The rapid inflation of an escape slide is achieved by a high-pressure gas canister combined with an aspirator. The gas release creates a venturi effect that draws in a large volume of air to inflate the slide in seconds.

question_text: Smoke detector systems are installed in the
option_a: upper cargo compartments (class E).
option_c: engine nacelles.
option_d: fuel tanks.
explanation: Cargo compartments of Class E are equipped with smoke detection systems. They are not installed in areas like engine nacelles or wheel wells, which use fire/overheat detectors rather than smoke detectors.

question_text: Ion detectors are devices used in aircraft for systems protection. They detect :
option_a: smoke.
option_c: fire.
option_d: overtemperature and fire.
explanation: Ionization smoke detectors are highly sensitive devices used in aircraft cabin and cargo compartments. They detect the presence of combustion particles (smoke) by measuring the change in electrical current across an ionized air chamber.

question_text: Smoke detectors fitted on transport aircraft are of the following type :
option_a: optical or ionization
option_c: electrical
option_d: magnetic
explanation: The two primary types of smoke detectors used in commercial aircraft cargo compartments and lavatories are optical detectors and ionization detectors. Both provide rapid warning of smoldering fires.

question_text: (For this question use annex 021-10164A)The smoke detection in the aircraft cargo compartments is carried out by four sensors: C1, C2, C3 and C4.They are associated with the logic circuit as described in the annex.The repeating bell is activated when:
option_a: the C1 and C2 sensors detect smoke.
option_b: the C1 and C3 sensors detect smoke.
option_c: only one sensor detects smoke.
option_d: the C2 and C4 sensors detect smoke.
explanation: The warning system logic is typically designed with redundancy to prevent false alarms. The repeating bell will only trigger when specific combinations, such as both sensors in a dual-loop system (e.g., C1 and C2), detect smoke.

question_text: When a continuous element of a fire detection system is heated:1. its resistance decreases.2. its resistance increases.3. the leakage current increases.4. the leakage current decreases.The combination regrouping all the correct statements is :
explanation: A continuous loop fire detection system (such as Fenwal or Kidde) uses a sensing element whose electrical resistance decreases as temperature increases. When heated, this resistance drop allows a higher leakage current to flow, triggering the alarm.

question_text: A fault protection circuit in a fire detection system will:
option_a: inhibit the fire detector when the detection line is connected to ground.
option_b: activate the fire detection system when the detection line is connected to ground.
option_c: automatically initiate APU shutdown and fire extinguisher striker activation in the event of fire.
option_d: activate an alarm in the cockpit and in the landing gear bay for ground crew.
explanation: If a fire detection sensing element becomes physically damaged and short-circuits to the ground, the fault protection circuit will detect this ground fault and inhibit the fire alarm for that loop, preventing a false fire warning.

question_text: In a fire detection system with single-loop continuous components (with no fault protection), if the line is accidently grounded:
option_a: the fire alarm is triggered.
option_b: the power supply is cut off automatically.
option_c: there will be no effect on the system
option_d: the engine fire extinguisher striker is automatically activated.
explanation: In a simple, single-loop continuous element fire detection system that lacks ground fault protection, any accidental grounding of the sensing wire to the airframe is electrically interpreted as a decrease in resistance. Consequently, this ground fault will immediately trigger a false fire warning in the cockpit.

question_text: When a wire type fire system is tested:
option_a: the wiring and the warning are tested.
option_b: Only the warning function is tested.
option_c: a part of the wire is totally heated.
option_d: the wire is totally heated.
explanation: When a continuous wire-type fire detection system is tested using the cockpit test switch, the test circuit verifies the electrical continuity of the sensing loops and the integrity of the warning light and aural alarm systems, but it does not physically heat the sensing element itself.

question_text: A gaseous sensor/responder tube fire sensor is tested by
option_a: heating up the sensor with test power connection.
option_b: checking the continuity of the system with a test switch.
option_c: checking the wiring harness for faults but not the sensor.
option_d: checking the sensor with pressurized gas.
explanation: A gaseous sensor/responder tube fire detector contains gas-charged sensing elements. The test switch functions by electrically heating up a small internal heater coil inside the responder unit, causing the gas pressure to rise and trigger the pressure switch to verify proper sensor operation.

question_text: In transport aeroplanes overheat detection systems are installed in the:
option_a: landing gear bays / wheel wells.
option_c: fuel tanks.
option_d: tyres.
explanation: Overheat detection systems are critical in areas where high friction or heat sources exist without normal cooling air. Consequently, they are installed in landing gear bays (wheel wells) to detect overheating brakes or fires caused by retracting hot wheels.

question_text: The indication of the fire detection systems is performed by a:
option_a: warning light and a warning bell (or aural alert).
option_c: warning light.
option_d: gear warning.
explanation: Because a fire requires immediate attention from the flight crew, fire detection systems must provide both visual and auditory warnings. This is accomplished using a red master warning light on the glare shield and an engine-specific warning light, accompanied by a warning bell or aural alert.

question_text: On a multi-engined aircraft a fire detection system includes :
option_a: a warning light for each engine and a single alarm bell common to all engines
option_b: a single warning light but a separate alarm bell for each engine
option_c: a single warning light and a single alarm bell
option_d: both a warning light and an alarm bell unique to each engine
explanation: On multi-engine aircraft, the warning systems are designed so the crew can immediately identify the affected engine. The system features a separate, dedicated warning light for each engine (usually located inside the fire handle) but utilizes a single, shared warning bell common to all engines.

question_text: In order to enable a fire to be controlled as quickly as possible, the fire detectors are located in the highest risk compartments. Theses compartments are :1. the main landing gear wheel wells2. the fuel tanks3. the oil tanks4. the auxiliary power unit5. around the enginesThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: To ensure passenger safety, fire detectors are placed in the compartments carrying the highest risk of fire or heat generation. These critical areas are the main landing gear wheel wells (due to hot brakes), the auxiliary power unit (APU) compartment, and around the main engines.

question_text: Continuous loop fire detector systems operate on the principle that an increase in temperature produces :
option_a: a decrease in resistance
option_c: a decrease in the reference current
option_d: a decrease in pressure
explanation: Continuous-loop fire detectors function on the principle that the core insulation material undergoes a significant drop in electrical resistance as its temperature increases. This resistance decrease allows a higher current to flow between the center wire and outer tube, triggering the fire alarm.

question_text: A Continuous-Loop-Detector-System is a:
option_a: Fire detection system
option_c: Carbon dioxide warning system
option_d: Fire fighting system
explanation: A continuous-loop detector system is a type of fire detection system. It uses a flexible metal tube containing a temperature-sensitive core to monitor engine nacelles and APU compartments for excessive heat or flame.

question_text: On an aircraft provided with resistance and capacitance variation type fire detection loops, a fire alarm is initiated by a temperature increase detected:
option_a: at any isolated point of the loops or else generally on all the loops
option_b: only at an isolated point of the loops
option_c: only in a uniform way along the loops
option_d: on at least one loop
explanation: Continuous-loop detectors can detect a fire either when a small section is exposed to intense localized heat (causing a sharp resistance drop or capacitance change at that point) or when the entire loop is heated uniformly (such as by overall engine compartment overheating).

question_text: When a bimetallic strip is used as a switch in a fire detection loop, a fire alarm is triggered after a delay. The purpose of this delay is to:
option_a: avoid false alarms in case of vibrations
option_c: delay the triggering of the fire extinguinshers and increase their efficiency
option_d: wait for the triggering of the second fire detection loop in order to confirm the fire
explanation: When a bimetallic thermal switch is used in a fire detection loop, a small time delay is incorporated. This delay prevents brief contacts caused by mechanical vibrations or transient heat spikes from triggering false fire alarms.

question_text: The most common extinguishing agent used in gas turbine engine fire protection system is:
option_a: Freon.
option_c: CO2.
option_d: Powder.
explanation: The most common fire extinguishing agents used in built-in engine fire protection systems are halogenated hydrocarbons (Halons). These gaseous agents extinguish fires by chemically interrupting the combustion chain reaction.

question_text: If inflammable gaseous materials, like propane for example, are set on fire, the following extinguisher types should be used for fire fighting:
option_a: BCF and CO2 type extinguishers
option_c: Dry and water type extinguishers
option_d: CO2 and water type extinguishers
explanation: Gaseous fuels like propane represent Class B (flammable gas) fires. They should be fought using BCF (Halon) or carbon dioxide (CO2) extinguishers, which displace oxygen and inhibit the flame chemical reaction without conducting electricity.

question_text: The most suitable means for extinguishing a magnesium fire on the ground is :
option_a: sand.
option_c: carbon dioxide.
option_d: freon.
explanation: Magnesium is a highly reactive metal that burns at extremely high temperatures and reacts violently with water, carbon dioxide, or halon. Therefore, the only effective way to extinguish a magnesium fire on the ground is to smother it using dry sand or a specialized Class D dry powder agent.

question_text: In the cockpit of a transport airplane, at least one manual fire-extinguisher must be conveniently located containing :
option_a: halon.
option_c: water.
option_d: special fluids.
explanation: Aviation regulations require at least one hand-held fire extinguisher to be located in the cockpit, and it must contain Halon. Halon is required because it is non-conductive, leaves no residue, and is highly effective against both electrical and fuel fires.

question_text: (For this question use annex 021-9377A)When fire is detected on engine n°2, the fire shutoff handle n°2 is pulled and the extinguishing agent n°1 is discharged. This results in :
option_a: the discharge of fire extinguisher bottle n°1 and illumination of the DISCH (discharge) indicator lamp
option_b: the discharge of fire extinguisher bottle n°1 and illumination of the DISCH indicator lamp of agent n°1 on both engines
option_c: the discharge of fire extinguisher bottle n°1 and illumination of the DISCH indicator lamp of agent n°1 on engine no. and DISCH indicator lamp of agent n°2 on engine n°1
option_d: the discharge of fire extinguisher bottle n°2 and illumination of the DISCH indicator lamp of agent n°1 on engine n°1 and agent n°2 on engine n°2
explanation: In a two-engine aircraft, pulling fire handle #2 arms the discharge squibs. Pressing the discharge switch for Agent 1 will fire bottle #1, routing the extinguishing gas into engine nacelle #2, and illuminate the "DISCH" lamp on the panel.

question_text: Generally, when the fire handle of the fire-extinguishing system on an aircraft is pulled, the effects are :1. closing of the LP valve of the fuel system2. opening of the air bleed valves and HP valves on the engine concerned3. setting of extinguishing systems4. closing of the isolation and de-icing valves5. isolation of the associated electric current generators6. immediate discharge of extinguishing agentThe combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: Pulling the engine fire handle isolates the affected engine from the aircraft systems. It closes the low-pressure fuel valve, closes the engine bleed air valves, de-energizes and shuts off the hydraulic supply, and arms the fire extinguisher squibs.

question_text: With engine fire alarm activated, the extinguisher discharge:
option_a: is the pilot's task
option_c: is automatic after a delay to allow the pilot to stop the engine
option_d: does not need the engine to be stopped
explanation: Automatic fire extinguishing is not used for aircraft engines in flight because discharging the agent shuts down the engine and is irreversible. Therefore, discharging the fire bottles is always a manual task performed by the pilot after verifying the emergency.

question_text: The main feature of BCF fire extinguishers is that they :
option_a: act as flame inhibitors by absorbing the air's oxygen.
option_b: use the cooling effect created by the venturi during discharge.
option_c: are electrical conductors.
option_d: are highly corrosive particularly for aluminium alloys.
explanation: Bromochlorodifluoromethane (BCF, or Halon 1211) is a liquefied gas that acts as a powerful flame inhibitor. It extinguishes fires by chemically disrupting the combustion chain reaction at the molecular level, rather than simply smothering or cooling the fire.

question_text: An airplane whose maximum approved passenger seating configuration is 7 to 30 seats must be equipped with at least:
option_a: 1 hand fire-extinguisher conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_b: 2 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_c: 3 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_d: 4 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
explanation: Under airworthiness regulations, a transport category aircraft configured with 7 to 30 passenger seats must be equipped with at least 1 hand-held fire extinguisher in the passenger cabin.

question_text: An airplane whose maximum approved passenger seating configuration is 31 to 60 seats must be equipped with at least:
option_a: 2 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_b: 3 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_c: 4 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_d: 5 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
explanation: Commercial aircraft with a maximum passenger seating configuration of 31 to 60 seats are required by regulations to carry at least 2 hand-held fire extinguishers distributed throughout the passenger cabin.

question_text: An airplane whose maximum approved passenger seating configuration is 61 to 200 seats must be equipped with at least:
option_a: 3 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_b: 2 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_c: 4 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_d: 5 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
explanation: Transport aeroplanes with a passenger seating configuration of 61 to 200 seats must be equipped with at least 3 hand-held fire extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.

question_text: An airplane whose maximum approved passenger seating configuration is 201 to 300 seats must be equipped with at least:
option_a: 4 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_b: 3 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_c: 5 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_d: 6 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
explanation: Commercial aircraft with a passenger seating configuration of 201 to 300 seats must be equipped with at least 4 hand-held fire extinguishers distributed in the passenger cabin.

question_text: An airplane whose maximum approved passenger seating configuration is 301 to 400 seats must be equipped with at least:
option_a: 5 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_b: 4 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_c: 6 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_d: 3 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
explanation: Aircraft configured with a passenger cabin of 301 to 400 seats must carry at least 5 hand-held fire extinguishers in the passenger compartment to ensure adequate fire protection.

question_text: An airplane whose maximum approved passenger seating configuration is 401 to 500 seats must be equipped with at least:
option_a: 6 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_b: 5 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_c: 7 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_d: 8 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
explanation: For transport aircraft with a passenger capacity of 401 to 500 seats, safety regulations dictate that at least 6 hand-held fire extinguishers must be installed in the cabin.

question_text: An airplane whose maximum approved passenger seating configuration is 501 to 600 seats must be equipped with at least:
option_a: 7 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_b: 8 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_c: 6 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_d: 5 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
explanation: Commercial aircraft configured with 501 to 600 passenger seats must carry a minimum of 7 hand-held fire extinguishers distributed throughout the passenger cabin.

question_text: An airplane whose maximum approved passenger seating configuration is greater than 600 seats must be equipped with at least:
option_a: 8 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_b: 9 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_c: 7 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
option_d: 6 hand fire-extinguishers conveniently located in the passenger compartment.
explanation: For very large transport aircraft configured with more than 600 passenger seats, safety standards require at least 8 hand-held fire extinguishers to be installed in the passenger cabin.

question_text: An airplane whose maximum approved passenger seating configuration is greater than 60 seats must be equipped with at least:
option_a: 3 HALON 1211 fire-extinguishers.
option_c: 4 HALON 1211 fire-extinguishers.
option_d: 1 HALON 1211 fire-extinguisher.
explanation: Commercial transport aircraft with a seating configuration of more than 60 passenger seats must have at least 3 of their hand-held extinguishers containing Halon 1211 (BCF) as the extinguishing agent.

question_text: In accordance with JAR-OPS 1, an airplane whose maximum take-off mass exceeds 5 700 kg or whose maximum approved passenger seating configuration is greater than 9 seats and smaller than 200 seats must be equipped with a:
option_a: crash axe or a crow-bar in the pilot compartment.
option_b: crash axe and a crow-bar in the passenger compartment.
option_c: crash axe in the cockpit and a crow-bar in the passenger compartment.
option_d: crow-bar in the cockpit and a crash axe in the passenger compartment.
explanation: In accordance with operating regulations, any aircraft with a maximum takeoff weight exceeding 5,700 kg or configured with more than 9 seats must be equipped with a crash axe or crowbar, which must be stored in the pilot compartment (cockpit).

question_text: In accordance with JAR-OPS 1, an airplane must be equipped with equipment or systems at each emergency exit that allow to reach the ground safely in the case of an emergency when the sill height of the passenger emergency exit is higher than:
explanation: Aircraft emergency exits must be fitted with evacuation assistance equipment (such as slides) if the door threshold or sill height is higher than 1.83 metres (6 feet) above the ground when the aircraft is on the ground with the landing gear extended.

question_text: In accordance with JAR-OPS 1, during and following an emergency descent, each occupant of the cockpit seats on duty must have access to a minimum amount of oxygen in:1. order to maintain a supply throughout the entire flight time where the cabin altitude pressure is greater than 13000 ft.2. order to maintain a supply throughout the entire flight time where the cabin altitude pressure is greater than 10000 ft and smaller than 13000 ft minus 30 minutes.3. no case less than 30 minutes for airplanes certified to fly up to 25000 ft.4. no case less than 2 hours for airplanes certified to fly at over 25000 ft.The combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: Operating regulations require that pressurized aircraft carry sufficient oxygen for the flight crew. This includes a supply for all flight crew members on duty for the entire flight time that the cabin altitude is above 10,000 ft, and not less than 2 hours for flights certified above 25,000 ft.

question_text: In accordance with JAR-OPS 1, the minimum requirement for the survival oxygen needed to supply 100 % of the passengers during and following an emergency descend is:
option_a: 10 minutes or the entire flight time where the cabin pressure altitude is above 15000 ft, whichever is the greater.
option_c: the entire flight time where the cabin pressure altitude is above 13000 ft.
option_d: the entire flight time where the cabin pressure altitude is above 10000 ft minus 30 minutes.
explanation: To protect passengers during a decompression event, the aircraft must carry enough oxygen to supply 100% of the passengers for at least 10 minutes, or for the entire flight duration when the cabin pressure altitude exceeds 15,000 ft, whichever is greater.

question_text: The oxygen masks have dropped down from the passengers service units. The oxygen flow starts :
option_a: after pulling the oxygen mask downwards
option_c: only above FL200
option_d: After the system has been switched on by a crew member
explanation: Once the passenger oxygen masks drop from the overhead panels, the flow of oxygen does not start automatically. The passenger must pull the mask downwards, which pulls a lanyard that releases the firing pin on the chemical generator.

question_text: A public transport jet aeroplane may be operated up to FL 450. The cabin includes 180 passenger seats, made up of 30 rows (3 seats from each side of central aisle). The minimum number of cabin oxygen masks for this aeroplane must be:
option_a: 198 (110% of the seating capacity).
option_c: 240 (one additional mask per seat block).
option_d: 210 (one additional mask per seat row).
explanation: To ensure that passenger service units (PSUs) have enough masks for lap children or crew members in the cabin aisle, regulations require that there be 10% more masks than seats. For a 180-seat aircraft, this requires at least 198 masks.

question_text: When quick donning masks are in use, the pilot is:
option_a: able to radiotelephone.
option_c: only able to transmit.
option_d: not able to do any radio communication.
explanation: Quick-donning oxygen masks used by the flight crew are equipped with an integrated microphone. This design ensures that the pilot is fully able to conduct two-way radiotelephone communications with ATC and other crew members while wearing the mask.

question_text: In a pressurized aircraft, the first-aid (therapeutic) oxygen is designed to:
option_a: give medical assistance to passengers with pathological respiratory disorders.
option_b: protect the flight crew and cabin attendants against fumes and noxious gases.
option_c: protect all the occupants against the effects of accidental depressurisation.
option_d: protect certain passengers, and is only carried on board for these people.
explanation: First-aid (or therapeutic) oxygen is dedicated oxygen carried on board pressurized transport aircraft. It is designed to provide medical assistance and breathing support to passengers suffering from pathological respiratory disorders or hypoxia after a decompression.

question_text: An aircraft is scheduled to fly from PARIS to MARSEILLE at FL 390 and has the following characteristics:Maximum permissible number of passenger specified by the certificate of airworthiness= 230Number of seats on board= 200Scheduled number of passengers on board= 180The minimum number of inhaler systems provided in the aircraft cabin should be:
explanation: Passenger oxygen systems must provide sufficient outlets to cover 110% of the total seats installed in the cabin to accommodate infants and crew. For a cabin fitted with 200 seats, this requires a minimum of 220 oxygen dispensing units or outlets.

question_text: From which flight level do the regulations require a quick donning type oxygen mask for the flight crew in a pressurized aircraft ?
explanation: Airworthiness regulations dictate that the flight crew in a pressurized aircraft must have access to quick-donning type oxygen masks that can be put on with one hand in under 5 seconds, when operating above Flight Level 250 (FL 250).

question_text: What is breathed in when using a passenger oxygen mask?
option_a: Cabin air and oxygen.
option_c: Cabin air and oxygen or 100% oxygen.
option_d: A mixture of oxygen and freon gas.
explanation: Passenger oxygen masks are constant-flow rebreather masks. They deliver pure oxygen into a reservoir bag, and when the passenger inhales, they breathe in a mixture of this supplied oxygen and ambient cabin air drawn through the mask's check valves.

question_text: The safety precautions to be taken whenever using oxygen are:1. refrain from smoking, avoid sparkes.2. Avoid operation of radio communication equipment.3. Slowly operate oxygen system valves.4. Avoid greasy matter.The combination regrouping all the correct statements is :
explanation: Oxygen is a powerful oxidizer that dramatically accelerates combustion. Safe handling precautions require that users refrain from smoking, avoid greasy substances or grease on tools, and open system valves slowly.

question_text: The opening of the doors giving access to the oxygen masks for the passengers is :1. pneumatic for the gaseous oxygen system,2. electrical for the chemical oxygen system,3. pneumatic for the chemical oxygen system,4. electrical for the gaseous oxygen system.The combination regrouping all the correct statements is:
explanation: The overhead passenger service unit (PSU) doors are released automatically during decompression. For gaseous oxygen systems, the doors are typically released pneumatically by system pressure; for chemical oxygen systems, the doors are released electrically.

question_text: The state in which the breathing oxygen for the cockpit of jet transport aeroplanes is stored is :
option_a: Gaseous.
option_c: Liquid.
option_d: Gaseous or chemical compound..
explanation: The flight crew's oxygen supply in jet transport aircraft is stored in its high-pressure gaseous state in cylinders. This allows the diluter-demand regulator to supply 100% oxygen or a mixture on demand, which is not possible with chemical generators.

question_text: If the maximum operating pressure of the oxygen system is exceeded the:
option_a: oxygen is discharged overboard via a safety plug.
option_b: oxygen becomes unusable for the passengers.
option_c: passenger oxygen masks will drop down.
option_d: oxygen bottles will explode.
explanation: If the pressure inside the oxygen storage cylinders exceeds safe limits due to thermal expansion, a safety relief valve opens. This discharges the high-pressure oxygen overboard through a dedicated blowout line.

question_text: The purpose of a diluter demand regulator in an oxygen system is to :
option_a: deliver oxygen flow when inhaling.
option_b: deliver oxygen flow only above FL 100.
option_c: is only recommended with smoke in the cockpit.
option_d: mix air and oxygen in a passenger oxygen mask.
explanation: The diluter-demand regulator used by the flight crew is designed to supply oxygen only when the user inhales (demand). It automatically dilutes the oxygen with ambient cabin air at lower altitudes and increases the oxygen concentration as cabin altitude rises.

question_text: The built-in passenger oxygen system be activated by :
option_a: switching the passenger oxygen ON.
option_b: switching the diluter demand regulator ON.
option_c: opening the oxygen-bottle valves.
option_d: switching the diluter demand regulator and the passenger oxygen ON.
explanation: The passenger oxygen system can be manually activated by the flight crew using a switch on the overhead panel, or it will deploy automatically when the cabin pressure altitude exceeds 14,000 feet, releasing the mask doors.

question_text: The passenger oxygen mask will supply :
option_a: a mixture of cabin air and oxygen.
option_c: a mixture of compressed air and oxygen or 100 % oxygen.
option_d: a mixture of oxygen and freon gas.
explanation: The yellow passenger mask is a simple continuous-flow mask. When the user inhales, they receive a mixture of pure oxygen from the reservoir bag and ambient cabin air that enters through diluter ports in the mask.
